gains-from-trade.title: Comparative Advantage and Gains from Trade
gains-from-trade.description: Analyze comparative advantage, specialization, mutually beneficial terms of trade, and the distribution of gains from exchange.

easy.q: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
options: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient.
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore
easy.commonError: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
easy.feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

easy.q: Mira gives up 1 report to prepare a presentation; Sol gives up 3 reports. Which fact determines comparative advantage in presentations?
options: Mira gives up fewer reports per presentation
Sol may complete more total tasks in a day
Mira charges a lower money price after exchange
Sol has a higher wage in an unrelated job
easy.commonError: Using total output, wages, or prices instead of opportunity cost.
easy.feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the lower-opportunity-cost producer.

easy.q: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
options: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop.
West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange
easy.commonError: Inferring comparative advantage from productivity alone.
easy.feedback: Greater output from the same resources establishes absolute, not necessarily comparative, advantage.

easy.q: Why can two people gain from trade even when one is better at producing both goods?
options: The less productive person must accept a loss.
Absolute advantage guarantees equal output.
Their opportunity costs can still differ.
Trade removes the need to specialize.
easy.commonError: Assuming the more productive producer should make everything.
easy.feedback: Different opportunity costs create room for specialization and mutually beneficial exchange.

easy.q: Specialization based on comparative advantage tends to:
options: Make both producers self-sufficient.
Require identical opportunity costs.
Prevent either side from consuming outside its PPF.
Increase the combined output available for exchange.
easy.feedback: When each producer concentrates on the lower-opportunity-cost good, combined output can rise.

easy.q: Voluntary trade occurs most directly because:
options: Each side expects the exchange to improve its situation.
One side must be forced to surrender a good.
Both sides must value the goods equally.
Prices must be fixed by a government.
easy.commonError: Thinking one side must lose whenever the other gains.
easy.feedback: A voluntary exchange happens when both parties expect to gain.

easy.q: Ana gives up 2 baskets to make one table; Bo gives up 5 baskets. Who has comparative advantage in tables?
options: Ana, because she gives up fewer baskets
Bo, because he gives up more baskets
Ana only if she makes more of both goods
Neither, because money prices are missing
easy.commonError: Confusing productivity or price with the relevant opportunity-cost rule.
easy.feedback: Comparative advantage is determined by relative opportunity cost.

easy.q: One worker can finish more of both tasks than a coworker. Why might the coworker still specialize in one task?
options: The coworker may have the lower opportunity cost in that task
The faster worker should perform both tasks because they produce more of each.
Comparative advantage requires equal productivity
Specialization removes every tradeoff
easy.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
easy.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

easy.q: Priya gives up 1 design to write a report; Luis gives up 4 designs. If they specialize by comparative advantage, who writes reports?
options: Priya, because her opportunity cost is lower
Luis, because his opportunity cost is higher
Both must split report writing equally
Whoever has the higher total output in both tasks
easy.commonError: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
easy.feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

easy.q: Why can specialization according to comparative advantage expand what two producers can consume?
options: It can increase combined production available for exchange
It guarantees each producer can make every good more efficiently.
It makes opportunity costs identical
It removes scarcity from both producers
easy.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
easy.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

medium.q: Rina can make 8 posters or 4 videos in a day. Malik can make 6 posters or 6 videos. Who has the comparative advantage in posters?
options: Malik, because he can make more videos.
Rina, because one poster costs her 0.5 video while it costs Malik 1 video.
Malik, because one poster costs him fewer posters.
Neither, because comparative advantage requires equal productivity.
medium.commonError: Comparing absolute output instead of opportunity costs.
medium.feedback: Rina gives up fewer videos per poster, so she has the comparative advantage in posters.

medium.q: Nora can edit 12 pages or design 3 graphics per hour. Eli can edit 8 pages or design 4 graphics. Who has the comparative advantage in graphics?
options: Nora, because she edits more pages.
Nora, because one graphic costs her fewer graphics.
Eli, because one graphic costs him 2 edited pages rather than Nora’s 4.
Neither, because Eli has no absolute advantage in editing.
medium.commonError: Using the higher total output as the comparative-advantage test.
medium.feedback: Eli sacrifices 2 edited pages per graphic; Nora sacrifices 4.

medium.q: Farm A can produce 20 crates of apples or 10 crates of pears. Farm B can produce 12 crates of apples or 12 crates of pears. Which specialization pattern follows comparative advantage?
options: Farm A specializes in pears and Farm B in apples.
Both farms specialize in apples because apples output is larger.
Neither farm specializes because both can produce both goods.
Farm A specializes relatively more in apples and Farm B in pears.
medium.commonError: Choosing specialization from absolute quantities alone.
medium.feedback: Farm A gives up 0.5 pear per apple; Farm B gives up 1 pear per apple.

medium.q: Ava gives up 2 cups of coffee to bake one loaf. Ben gives up 5 cups to bake one loaf. A trade price of one loaf for 3 cups of coffee is:
options: Potentially beneficial to both Ava and Ben.
Beneficial only to Ava.
Beneficial only to Ben.
Outside the mutually beneficial range.
medium.commonError: Failing to place the trading price between the two opportunity costs.
medium.feedback: Three cups lies between Ava’s cost of 2 and Ben’s cost of 5 cups per loaf.

medium.q: Country X gives up 3 tons of wheat for one machine. Country Y gives up 7 tons. Which statement is correct?
options: Country Y has the comparative advantage in machines.
Country X has the comparative advantage in machines.
Country X must also have the comparative advantage in wheat.
Comparative advantage cannot be identified from opportunity costs.
medium.commonError: Assigning comparative advantage to the higher opportunity-cost producer.
medium.feedback: Country X sacrifices less wheat per machine.

medium.q: After specialization, total production rises but one proposed trade leaves a producer worse off. What failed?
options: Comparative advantage ceased to exist.
Specialization always lowers total output.
The proposed terms of trade were not mutually beneficial.
Absolute advantage made exchange impossible.
medium.commonError: Assuming higher total output makes every possible trade acceptable.
medium.feedback: Specialization can create gains, but the exchange terms must divide those gains so both sides benefit.

medium.q: Team A can prepare 12 briefs or 6 charts daily. Team B can prepare 8 briefs or 8 charts. Who has comparative advantage in briefs?
options: Team A; one brief costs 0.5 chart rather than 1 chart
Team B; it can make more charts.
Team A; it has comparative advantage in both outputs
Neither; their maximum outputs differ
medium.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
medium.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

medium.q: Kai needs 2 hours per cabinet and 1 hour per shelf. Ren needs 3 hours per cabinet and 3 hours per shelf. Who has comparative advantage in cabinets?
options: Kai; a cabinet costs 2 shelves rather than Ren’s 1 shelf
Ren; a cabinet costs 1 shelf rather than Kai’s 2 shelves
Kai; fewer hours always means comparative advantage in both goods
Neither; hours per unit cannot reveal opportunity cost
medium.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
medium.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

medium.q: If one mug costs a studio 2 bowls, what is the reciprocal opportunity cost of one bowl?
options: One-half mug
Two mugs.
Four mugs
One mug
medium.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
medium.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

medium.q: Farm C can grow 24 corn or 12 beans; Farm D can grow 10 corn or 10 beans. Which specialization follows comparative advantage?
options: Farm C grows corn and Farm D grows beans
Farm C grows beans and Farm D grows corn
Both farms grow only corn
Neither farm can specialize without a money price
medium.commonError: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
medium.feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

medium.q: One lamp costs Ari 2 rugs and costs Bea 6 rugs. Which rate for 1 lamp could provide strict gains to both?
options: 4 rugs per lamp
2 rugs per lamp
6 rugs per lamp
8 rugs per lamp
medium.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
medium.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

medium.q: Two workshops each give up exactly 3 frames to produce one desk. What does the basic model imply?
options: Neither has comparative advantage in desks based on these costs
The workshop with greater desk output must specialize in desks.
Both receive strict gains from any desk price
One workshop must have comparative advantage in both goods
medium.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
medium.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

hard.q: Jordan can prepare 6 tax returns or 3 financial plans. Casey can prepare 8 tax returns or 8 plans. If they specialize efficiently, what should happen?
options: Jordan concentrates on plans and Casey on returns.
Casey produces both because Casey has absolute advantage in both.
They split both tasks equally because specialization requires equal output.
Jordan concentrates on tax returns and Casey on financial plans.
hard.commonError: Letting absolute advantage determine both specialization choices.
hard.feedback: Jordan gives up 0.5 plan per return; Casey gives up 1 plan per return.

hard.q: Island A can produce 30 fish or 10 baskets. Island B can produce 18 fish or 9 baskets. Which trade price for one basket could benefit both?
options: Between 2 and 3 fish per basket.
Less than 1 fish per basket only.
More than 4 fish per basket only.
Exactly 9 fish per basket.
hard.commonError: Using output levels rather than opportunity-cost bounds.
hard.feedback: A basket costs A 3 fish and B 2 fish, so a mutually beneficial price lies between them.

hard.q: Maya is faster than Leo at both coding and testing. Why might Maya still assign testing to Leo?
options: Absolute advantage requires Maya to do both tasks.
Leo may have the lower opportunity cost of testing.
Testing cannot be traded within a team.
Maya’s wage automatically determines comparative advantage.
hard.commonError: Assuming the most productive worker should perform every task.
hard.feedback: Efficient assignment depends on relative sacrifice, not only speed.

hard.q: Two regions specialize according to comparative advantage, but transport costs exceed the production gains. What is the best conclusion?
options: Comparative advantage is mathematically impossible.
Absolute advantage has replaced opportunity cost.
The gross gains from specialization may be smaller than the costs of exchange.
Trade must still make both regions better off.
hard.feedback: Comparative advantage identifies production gains, but real exchange costs can erase net gains.

hard.q: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
options: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade.
The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident
hard.commonError: Preferring self-sufficiency without comparing opportunity costs.
hard.feedback: Exchange uses resources worth 3 tons rather than 5, freeing 2 tons for other uses.

hard.q: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
Comparative advantage is disproved whenever gains are unequal.
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output
hard.commonError: Confusing total gains with mutual benefit under a particular exchange.
hard.feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

hard.q: River can produce 18 X or 6 Y; Hill can produce 12 X or 8 Y. What are their reciprocal costs of 1 Y?
options: River: 3 X; Hill: 1.5 X
River: one-third X; Hill: two-thirds X
River: 12 X; Hill: 18 X
River: 2 X; Hill: 3 X
hard.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
hard.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

hard.q: North can make 20 chips or 10 sensors; South can make 12 chips or 12 sensors. A technology change lets North make 40 sensors with unchanged chip capacity. What changes?
options: North gains comparative advantage in sensors and South in chips
North keeps comparative advantage in chips because its chip output is unchanged
South gains comparative advantage in both goods
Equal opportunity costs eliminate specialization
hard.commonError: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
hard.feedback: Recompute relative opportunity costs after a change and respect the model limits.

hard.q: Ava’s cost of one crate is 2 sacks; Ben’s is 5 sacks. At exactly 2 sacks per crate, which statement is correct?
options: Ava is indifferent and Ben can gain from buying the crate
Both receive strict gains from the trade.
Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs
hard.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
hard.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

hard.q: One bolt costs East 0.5 panel and West 1.25 panels. Which interval states strict mutual-gain rates in panels per bolt?
options: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
More than 2 but less than 4 bolts per panel.
At least 0.5 and at most 1.25 panels per bolt
Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only
hard.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
hard.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

hard.q: A consultant completes more audits and presentations than an associate. A manager concludes the consultant should do both. What is missing?
options: The opportunity cost of assigning the consultant to each task
Only the consultant’s total output in both tasks.
A guarantee that specialization divides gains equally
The money price of international exports
hard.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
hard.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

hard.q: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
options: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
Every feasible exchange must share the production gain.
The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred
hard.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
hard.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

elite.q: Producer A sacrifices 0.25 units of Y for one X; Producer B sacrifices 0.40 units of Y. Which statement is most precise?
options: A has comparative advantage in both goods.
A has comparative advantage in X, while B has comparative advantage in Y.
B has comparative advantage in X because 0.40 is larger.
No comparative advantage exists without money prices.
elite.commonError: Forgetting that comparative advantage in one good implies the other producer has it in the other good.
elite.feedback: A has the lower cost of X; reciprocally, B has the lower cost of Y.

elite.q: Two producers have identical opportunity costs for both goods. What does the basic two-good model predict?
options: Both gain automatically from complete specialization.
The producer with absolute advantage must import both goods.
No gains from specialization based solely on comparative advantage.
Any terms of trade will double total output.
elite.commonError: Assuming trade gains arise even without relative-cost differences.
elite.feedback: Identical opportunity costs leave no comparative-advantage basis for specialization.

elite.q: A trade rate equals the exporter’s opportunity cost exactly but remains below the importer’s opportunity cost. Which evaluation is precise?
options: The exporter is indifferent while the importer captures the modeled gain
The exporter captures every gain because it supplies the good.
Both parties receive strict and exactly equal gains
Neither party can gain because the rate is on one boundary
elite.commonError: Calling a boundary rate a strict mutual gain or assuming gains divide equally.
elite.feedback: At its own opportunity cost the exporter is indifferent; the importer still saves resources.

elite.q: When productivity changes, comparative advantage can shift because:
options: The relevant opportunity-cost ratios can change.
Absolute output can never affect relative costs.
Trade prices permanently fix specialization.
Comparative advantage is determined by population size alone.
elite.feedback: Technology, skills, and institutions can change relative productivity and opportunity costs.

elite.q: A can make 12 X or 24 Y and B can make 10 X or 10 Y. After full specialization, B sends A 4 X for 6 Y. A previously consumed 4 X and 12 Y. What is A's gain?
options: The same 4 X and 6 additional Y
Four additional X and the same Y
Six additional X and 4 additional Y
No gain because A exports output
elite.commonError: Comparing a post-trade bundle with specialization output instead of the stated autarky bundle.
elite.feedback: Subtract the stated autarky bundle from post-trade consumption good by good.

elite.q: C can make 16 cloth or 8 wine; D can make 6 cloth or 12 wine. They fully specialize, and C trades 4 cloth for 4 wine. Before trade, C consumed 12 cloth and 2 wine while D consumed 2 cloth and 8 wine. What are the gains?
options: C gains 2 wine; D gains 2 cloth
C gains 4 wine; D gains 4 cloth
C gains 2 cloth; D gains 2 wine
Each gains 2 units of both goods
elite.commonError: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
elite.feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

legendary.q: With constant tradeoffs, Forge can make 36 panels or 12 motors; Harbor can make 20 panels or 10 motors. Forge imports a motor and pays an additional shipping cost of 0.5 panel per motor. Which quoted panel price gives both strict gains?
options: 3 panels per motor
2.25 panels per motor
2 panels per motor
2.75 panels per motor
legendary.feedback: Forge's domestic cost is 3 panels; Harbor's is 2. Harbor requires a price above 2, while Forge requires price + 0.5 below 3. Only 2.25 is strictly between 2 and 2.5.

legendary.q: A high-productivity surgeon is also the fastest typist in a clinic. The surgeon hires an assistant to type notes. What completes the economic explanation?
options: The assistant must have an absolute advantage in typing.
The surgeon cannot have comparative advantage in surgery.
The surgeon’s opportunity cost of typing is high because typing displaces valuable surgical time.
Specialization matters only in international trade.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring the value of the next-best use of time.
legendary.feedback: The surgeon delegates typing because the forgone value of surgical work makes typing costly for the surgeon.

legendary.q: Country A has comparative advantage in software. After trade opens, software employment rises but some hardware workers lose jobs. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The job losses prove comparative advantage was calculated incorrectly.
All workers must gain for trade to be efficient.
Comparative advantage predicts no sectoral adjustment.
Aggregate gains can coexist with transition costs and distributional losses.
legendary.commonError: Treating aggregate efficiency and distribution as the same criterion.
legendary.feedback: Trade can expand total gains while requiring adjustment and creating identifiable losers.

legendary.q: Suppose learning-by-doing lowers a nation’s future opportunity cost in a good it does not currently produce. What does this imply?
options: Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
Opportunity costs can never change over time.
The nation must already have absolute advantage in that good.
Trade eliminates any reason to consider future productivity.
legendary.commonError: Assuming the static model settles every long-run policy question.
legendary.feedback: Investment and learning can alter future relative costs, so dynamic considerations may matter.

legendary.q: Two firms specialize and increase combined output by 20 units, but contracting and monitoring cost 25 units. What follows?
options: Comparative advantage does not exist.
The specialization creates gross gains but a net loss after transaction costs.
The firms must trade because output rose.
Transaction costs are transfers and cannot affect net gains.
legendary.commonError: Ignoring costs of arranging and enforcing exchange.
legendary.feedback: Net gains equal production gains minus the real costs of coordinating trade.

legendary.q: A country can import steel for 4 units of wheat per ton. Producing a ton domestically costs 6 units of wheat. Which statement is best?
options: Domestic steel has lower opportunity cost.
The money price alone proves dumping.
Importing steel frees 2 units of wheat-equivalent resources per ton for other uses.
Importing steel reduces available resources by 2 units per ton.
legendary.commonError: Comparing domestic and foreign choices without a common opportunity-cost measure.
legendary.feedback: Importing at a cost of 4 instead of producing at a cost of 6 releases resources worth 2 units of wheat.

legendary.q: A workshop's cost of a motor is 2 batteries; its trading partner's is 5. The workshop exports motors and pays 1 battery in shipping per motor. In motors per battery, which strict price range benefits both?
options: Between 1/5 and 1/3 motor per battery
Between 1/5 and 1/2 motor per battery
Between 3 and 5 motors per battery
Between 1/3 and 1/2 motor per battery
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: The battery price must exceed 2 + 1 = 3 for the exporter and remain below 5 for the importer. Reciprocating reverses the bounds: 1/5 < motors per battery < 1/3.

legendary.q: After specializing, a workshop has 30 panels. It can trade panels for motors at 3 panels per motor. Its former bundle was 16 panels and 3 motors. Which integer trade leaves it with strictly more of both goods?
options: Trade 12 panels for 4 motors
Trade 9 panels for 3 motors
Trade 15 panels for 5 motors
Trade 6 panels for 2 motors
legendary.commonError: Comparing a post-trade bundle with specialization output instead of the stated autarky bundle.
legendary.feedback: Trading 12 leaves 18 panels and 4 motors, above both former quantities. Nine panels only matches former motors; fifteen leaves too few panels; six leaves fewer motors.

legendary.q: North specializes at 24 fish and South at 12 nets. North trades 8 fish for 4 nets. Their autarky bundles were North 12 fish and 3 nets, South 6 fish and 6 nets. What are their gains?
options: North gains 4 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
North gains 8 fish and 4 nets; South gains 8 fish and 4 nets
North gains 4 fish and 4 nets; South gains 2 fish and 6 nets
North gains 12 fish and 1 net; South gains 2 fish and 2 nets
legendary.commonError: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
legendary.feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

legendary.q: One printer costs X 3 scanners and Y 7 scanners. X exports a printer at a quoted price of 6 scanners but Y must also use 2 scanners for shipping. What would make both strictly better off?
options: A quoted price strictly between 3 and 5 scanners
Any quoted price strictly between 3 and 7 scanners
The existing price of 6 because it is below Y's domestic cost
A price of 7 because it exactly matches Y's production cost
legendary.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
legendary.feedback: X needs a quote above 3. Y's full import cost is quote + 2, which must be below 7. Thus 3 < quote < 5; ignoring shipping overstates the mutual-gain range.

legendary.q: Specialization yields 14 extra units. Under one exchange, Metro gains 10 units while Harbor gains 4. Which conclusion is accurate?
options: Both gain, but the terms divide the gain unequally
Unequal gains mean Harbor cannot benefit.
Each side must gain 7 units
Only Metro has comparative advantage
legendary.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
legendary.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

legendary.q: At constant tradeoffs, Oak can make 24 racks or 8 desks; Pine can make 18 racks or 9 desks. Oak adopts a tool that raises its desk maximum to 16 without changing racks. Which conclusion follows?
options: Oak switches to comparative advantage in desks; a 1.75-rack desk price can then benefit both
Pine retains desk advantage because its rack maximum is lower
Oak has comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima exceed Pine's
The old 2.5-rack desk price still gives Oak strict gains when it imports desks
legendary.commonError: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
legendary.feedback: Oak's desk cost falls from 3 to 1.5 racks; Pine's stays 2. Oak becomes the lower-cost desk maker, and 1.75 lies between their costs. At the old import price Oak could now make desks more cheaply.

legendary.q: With constant tradeoffs, Ridge can make 24 maps or 12 models. Vale can make 18 maps or m models. Ridge exports models at 1.5 maps each and claims both gain strictly. Which value of m makes the claim consistent?
options: No positive m; Ridge loses at the stated export price
m = 6; Vale's higher cost suffices for mutual gains
m = 9; matching costs makes this price mutually beneficial
m = 18; Vale's higher model productivity guarantees mutual gains
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Ridge sacrifices 2 maps to make a model but receives only 1.5 maps. Regardless of Vale's productivity, Ridge loses on this export; solving only Vale's inequality misses one side.

legendary.q: Coast's cost of 1 cocoa is 3 tea. Ridge's is 6 tea. Expressed as cocoa per tea, which strict range is equivalent?
options: More than one-sixth and less than one-third
More than one-third and less than one-sixth
More than 3 and less than 6
At least one-sixth and at most one-third
legendary.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
legendary.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

legendary.q: Two labs each sacrifice 4 tests for one prototype at constant tradeoffs. One lab doubles its maximum output of both goods. What changes in the pure comparative-advantage model?
options: Its capacity rises, but equal opportunity costs still leave no strict specialization gains at any common price
It gains comparative advantage in both goods because both maxima double
A price of 4 tests now gives both a strict gain on each prototype
Doubling capacity halves its opportunity cost of a prototype
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Proportional productivity growth leaves the ratio unchanged. At 4 tests both are indifferent; any other price advantages one direction while making the other party worse off.

legendary.q: Specialization creates a gross gain of 24 units of a common consumption good. Shipping uses 5 units and verification uses 7. The proposed division gives one party 15 units of gross gain and assigns it both costs. Does that party gain, and what net gain remains for the other?
options: Yes, it gains 3 units; the other gains 9
Yes, it gains 15 units; the other gains 9
No, it loses 12 units; the other gains 24
Yes, both gain 12 units
legendary.commonError: Comparing a post-trade bundle with specialization output instead of the stated autarky bundle.
legendary.feedback: Net total gain is 24 - 5 - 7 = 12. The cost-paying party gains 15 - 12 = 3; the other receives the remaining gross 9 and pays no cost.

legendary.q: An engineer needs 2 hours per design and 1 hour per inspection. A technician needs 6 hours per design and 2 hours per inspection. They move one inspection from the engineer to the technician, who gives up one-third of a design. What net design capacity is freed?
options: One-sixth of a design
One-half of a design
One-third of a design
Five-sixths of a design
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: The engineer saves an hour, enough for half a design. The technician's two hours cost one-third of a design. Net capacity gain is 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6; the engineer's absolute inspection advantage does not settle assignment.

legendary.q: Mesa specializes at 30 meals and Bay at 15 repairs. Mesa trades 10 meals for 5 repairs. Their autarky bundles were Mesa 15 meals and 4 repairs, Bay 8 meals and 7 repairs. What gains result?
options: Mesa gains 5 meals and 1 repair; Bay gains 2 meals and 3 repairs
Mesa gains 10 meals and 5 repairs; Bay gains 10 meals and 5 repairs
Mesa gains 5 meals and 5 repairs; Bay gains 2 meals and 7 repairs
Mesa gains 15 meals and 1 repair; Bay gains 2 meals and 3 repairs
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

legendary.q: One machine costs Alpha 2 kits and Beta 6 kits. Compare rates of 3 and 5 kits per machine. Which statement is true?
options: Both work, but 5 shifts more modeled gain to Alpha
Only the 3-kit rate lies between the two opportunity costs.
Only the 5-kit rate is between costs
Both divide the gain equally
legendary.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
legendary.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

legendary.q: A problem gives specialization output and a trading rate but no pre-trade consumption bundle. Can a unique numerical consumption gain be found?
options: No; the autarky comparison is underdetermined
Yes; the trading rate determines the pre-trade consumption bundle.
Yes; combined output equals each gain
No; trade gains can never be measured
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

legendary.q: A technology has increasing rather than constant opportunity cost. Which claim is safest?
options: Comparative advantage can guide reallocation without universal complete specialization
Both producers must always specialize completely.
Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
Absolute advantage fixes every output
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

legendary.q: Combined consumption rises by 9 units, but one party gains 11 while the other loses 2. What is the correct evaluation?
options: Aggregate gain exists, but the trade is not mutually beneficial
Both parties gain because their combined consumption increases.
The losing party has advantage in both goods
Each gain must be reset to 4.5
legendary.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
legendary.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

legendary.q: Delta can make 24 files or 8 reviews; Echo can make 15 files or 10 reviews at constant tradeoffs. Delta doubles review productivity without changing files. A contract exchanges one review for 2 files. What changes?
options: The cost difference disappears, and the old contract no longer gives both strict gains
Delta gains review advantage because 16 exceeds Echo's 10
Echo retains review advantage because 15 is below Delta's 24 files
Both now gain strictly at every price between 1.5 and 3 files
legendary.commonError: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
legendary.feedback: Initially review costs are 3 and 1.5 files, so 2 can benefit both. Delta's new cost is 24/16 = 1.5, equal to Echo's. At 2, a review importer would pay more than domestic cost.

legendary.q: A lens costs Urban 0.25 sensor and Rural 0.5 sensor. Urban proposes exporting lenses at 3 lenses per sensor, and pays shipping of 0.05 sensor per lens. Which assessment is correct?
options: Both gain: Urban nets more than 0.25 sensor per lens and Rural pays less than 0.5
Urban loses because three is larger than both stated opportunity costs
Rural loses because the reciprocal price is above 0.5 sensor per lens
Both are indifferent because shipping makes the costs equal
legendary.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
legendary.feedback: The quote is 1/3 sensor per lens. Urban nets 1/3 - 0.05, about 0.283, above 0.25; Rural pays about 0.333, below 0.5. Keep price and cost in the same units.

legendary.q: Lumen specializes at 32 lamps and Shade at 16 rugs. Lumen trades 12 lamps for 6 rugs. Autarky bundles were Lumen 16 lamps and 4 rugs, Shade 8 lamps and 8 rugs. What results?
options: Lumen gains 4 lamps and 2 rugs; Shade gains 4 lamps and 2 rugs
Lumen gains 4 lamps and 6 rugs; Shade gains 4 lamps but loses 2 rugs
Lumen loses 4 lamps and gains 2 rugs; Shade gains 12 lamps and 2 rugs
Each gains only rugs
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

legendary.q: Before specialization, two workshops jointly consume 18 frames and 10 cushions. Specialization produces 23 frames and 13 cushions; transport uses 2 cushions. Which claim follows before the remaining goods are divided?
options: The available bundle rises by 5 frames and 1 cushion, but individual gains depend on the division
Both parties necessarily gain 5 frames and 1 cushion each
Net cushion gain is 3 because transport is separate from production
One party's loss is impossible whenever both aggregate quantities rise
legendary.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendary.feedback: After transport, 23 frames and 11 cushions remain, a net gain of 5 and 1. Aggregate improvement permits beneficial divisions but does not establish the gains of a particular division.

legendary.q: A static two-good model finds gains from specialization. Which conclusion goes beyond that result alone?
options: Every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry
Lower opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage.
Terms inside the bounds can create mutual gains
Specialization can raise output under the assumptions
legendary.commonError: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
legendary.feedback: The static model can show gains from specialization under its assumptions, but it does not establish that every long-run trade policy benefits every worker and industry.

boss.q: Which condition creates the basic possibility of gains from specialization?
options: Identical opportunity costs.
Equal money incomes.
A legal price floor.
Different opportunity costs.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: If each trader voluntarily accepts an exchange, what is the immediate inference?
options: Each expects to be better off from the trade.
Each must have equal productivity.
One trader has been made worse off.
Scarcity has ended.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: Who has comparative advantage in a task?
options: The person with the highest wage.
The person with the lower opportunity cost.
The person with the highest total output in every task.
The person who sets the market price.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: Lena gives up 1 report to make a presentation; Omar gives up 3 reports. Who should specialize relatively more in presentations?
options: Omar.
Both equally.
Lena.
Neither; absolute advantage is required.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: A trade price lies between the two producers’ opportunity costs. What does that imply?
options: Only the higher-cost producer can gain.
Neither can gain.
The price must be illegal.
Both can gain from the exchange.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: One producer is more productive in both goods. Why can trade still help?
options: Comparative advantage depends on relative opportunity costs.
Absolute advantage forces self-sufficiency.
The less productive producer has no cost.
Trade gains require equal output.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: A specialization plan raises total output but transport costs are even larger. What is the net result?
options: A guaranteed net gain.
A net loss despite gross production gains.
No opportunity costs.
Proof that specialization did not occur.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: Trade raises national surplus but harms one domestic industry. Which statement is accurate?
options: Every individual must gain.
Comparative advantage is disproved.
Efficiency gains and distributional losses can occur together.
The harmed industry must have comparative advantage.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: Technology lowers one country’s opportunity cost of a previously imported good. What may change?
options: The definition of scarcity.
The need for opportunity-cost comparison.
The existence of all trade gains.
Its pattern of comparative advantage.
boss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
boss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

boss.q: A baker makes more bread and cakes than a helper. What must be known before assigning both tasks?
options: Their opportunity costs for bread and cakes
Only the baker’s total output in both goods.
The price of imported flour
Whether the helper likes cake
boss.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
boss.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

boss.q: Nia gives up 2 posters per video; Omar gives up 5. Who should specialize in videos?
options: Nia, because her opportunity cost is lower
Omar, because he gives up more posters per video.
Both, because gains must be equal
Neither, because totals are missing
boss.commonError: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
boss.feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

boss.q: One drone costs East 1.5 radios and West 4 radios. At 1.5 radios per drone, what happens?
options: East is indifferent while West can gain
Both receive strict gains
West is indifferent while East can gain
The rate is strictly inside the bounds
boss.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
boss.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

boss.q: Two producers have equal opportunity costs for both goods. What does the basic model predict?
options: No comparative-advantage basis for usual specialization
The higher-output producer has comparative advantage in both goods.
Each must specialize in a different good
Every exchange produces strict gains
boss.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
boss.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

boss.q: A can produce 16 apples or 8 pears; B can produce 9 apples or 9 pears. Who has comparative advantage in apples?
options: A; one apple costs 0.5 pear
B; one apple costs 1 pear
A; it has advantage in both
Neither; only money costs count
boss.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
boss.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

boss.q: One file costs Town 3 reports and City 7 reports. Which rate can strictly benefit both?
options: 5 reports per file
3 reports per file
7 reports per file
9 reports per file
boss.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
boss.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

legendaryBoss.q: At constant tradeoffs, A makes 30 filters or 10 pumps; B makes 24 filters or 12 pumps. B exports pumps and pays shipping of 0.4 filter per pump. Which price gives both strict gains and gives B the larger per-pump gain measured in filters?
options: 2.8 filters per pump
2.5 filters per pump
2.4 filters per pump
3 filters per pump
legendaryBoss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
legendaryBoss.feedback: B's net gain is price - 2 - 0.4; A's is 3 - price. At 2.8 the gains are 0.4 and 0.2. At 2.5 A gains more; 2.4 or 3 leaves one party indifferent.

legendaryBoss.q: A manager is best at sales and bookkeeping but delegates bookkeeping. Which fact can justify the decision?
options: The assistant must be better at both tasks.
The manager sacrifices more valuable sales output when doing bookkeeping.
Absolute advantage prevents delegation.
Bookkeeping has no opportunity cost.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

legendaryBoss.q: A trade agreement creates $100 million in total gains and $30 million in adjustment costs. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Every affected worker gains.
The agreement creates no real costs.
Net gains are positive, but distribution and adjustment still matter.
Comparative advantage requires zero adjustment.
legendaryBoss.commonError: Choosing the wrong opportunity-cost or net-gain criterion.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Use opportunity cost and net benefits to evaluate specialization and exchange.

legendaryBoss.q: Arbor specializes at 28 timber and Basin at 14 tools. Arbor trades 8 timber for 4 tools. Autarky bundles were Arbor 14 timber and 3 tools, Basin 6 timber and 7 tools. What gains result?
options: Arbor gains 6 timber and 1 tool; Basin gains 2 timber and 3 tools
Arbor gains 8 timber and 4 tools; Basin gains 8 timber and 4 tools
Arbor gains 6 timber and 4 tools; Basin gains 2 timber and 7 tools
Arbor gains 14 timber and 1 tool; Basin gains 2 timber and 3 tools
legendaryBoss.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

legendaryBoss.q: A chip costs Quartz 2 screens and Sable 5 screens. Quartz offers 1 chip for 5 screens. Which result is precise?
options: Quartz gains while Sable is indifferent
Both receive strict and equal gains
Quartz is indifferent while Sable gains
Neither can gain at an integer rate
legendaryBoss.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

legendaryBoss.q: Cedar can make 30 boards or 10 doors; Dune can make 16 boards or 8 doors. A tool doubles Dune's board output. What specialization follows?
options: Dune makes boards; Cedar makes doors
Cedar makes boards; Dune makes doors
Cedar has advantage in both
Equal costs remove specialization
legendaryBoss.commonError: Treating comparative advantage as fixed after productivity or opportunity costs change.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Recompute relative opportunity costs after a change and respect the model limits.

legendaryBoss.q: Orchid specializes at 36 flowers and Reed at 18 baskets. Orchid trades 12 flowers for 6 baskets. Autarky bundles were Orchid 18 flowers and 4 baskets, Reed 9 flowers and 9 baskets. What gains result?
options: Orchid gains 6 flowers and 2 baskets; Reed gains 3 flowers and 3 baskets
Orchid gains 12 flowers and 6 baskets; Reed gains 12 flowers and 6 baskets
Orchid gains 6 flowers and 6 baskets; Reed gains 3 flowers and 9 baskets
Orchid gains 18 flowers and 2 baskets; Reed gains 3 flowers and 3 baskets
legendaryBoss.commonError: Using the wrong autarky bundle or failing to conserve the traded goods.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Derive both post-trade bundles and compare each with its stated autarky bundle.

legendaryBoss.q: One turbine costs Haven 3 grain and Isle 7 grain. Compare rates of 4 and 6 grain per turbine. Which shifts more gain toward Haven while benefiting both?
options: The 6-grain rate
The 4-grain rate
Neither rate is inside the bounds
Both divide gains identically
legendaryBoss.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

legendaryBoss.q: Peak specializes at 40 services and Glen at 20 devices. Peak trades 16 services for 8 devices. Autarky bundles were Peak 20 services and 6 devices, Glen 10 services and 10 devices. What gains result?
options: Peak gains 4 services and 2 devices; Glen gains 6 services and 2 devices
Peak gains 16 services and 8 devices; Glen gains 16 services and 8 devices
Peak gains 4 services and 8 devices; Glen gains 6 services and 10 devices
Peak loses 4 services while Glen gains 6 services
legendaryBoss.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
legendaryBoss.feedback: Work through the complete model in order and keep the ratio units fixed.

repairQuestions.q: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer who:
options: Produces the largest amount of every good.
Charges the lowest money price after trade.
Has the highest income.
Gives up less of the alternative good.
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing absolute productivity with comparative advantage.
repairQuestions.feedback: Compare opportunity costs, not total output.

repairQuestions.q: A mutually beneficial terms-of-trade price must generally lie:
options: Between the two producers’ opportunity costs.
Above both opportunity costs.
Below both opportunity costs.
At the higher producer’s total output.
repairQuestions.commonError: Not using opportunity costs as the trading-price bounds.
repairQuestions.feedback: A price between the opportunity costs lets both sides save resources.

repairQuestions.q: Trade can benefit both sides because:
options: One side is forced to accept a loss.
Specialization can increase combined output and exchange can share the gain.
Scarcity disappears after exchange.
Both sides must have identical skills.
repairQuestions.feedback: Voluntary specialization and exchange can create mutual gains.

repairQuestions.q: When two producers face different tradeoffs, which one holds comparative advantage in an activity?
options: The producer with lower opportunity cost
The producer who gives up more
The producer with the highest wage
The producer who makes most of everything
repairQuestions.commonError: Confusing productivity or price with the relevant opportunity-cost rule.
repairQuestions.feedback: Comparative advantage is determined by relative opportunity cost.

repairQuestions.q: If one producer makes more of both goods, must that producer make both?
options: No; specialization depends on relative opportunity costs
Yes; absolute advantage determines both assignments.
Yes; the slower producer should never produce
No; productivity data never matter
repairQuestions.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
repairQuestions.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

repairQuestions.q: If 1 X costs 2 Y, what is the cost of 1 Y?
options: One-half X
Two X.
Four X
One X
repairQuestions.commonError: Repeating a ratio instead of taking its reciprocal.
repairQuestions.feedback: Reverse both the goods and the ratio when changing opportunity-cost orientation.

repairQuestions.q: Does higher combined production make every proposed exchange beneficial?
options: No; the trading terms still determine who gains
Yes; every exchange shares the additional output.
Yes; gains are always equal
No; specialization cannot raise output
repairQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
repairQuestions.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

repairQuestions.q: A trading rate equals one producer's opportunity cost. Is that producer strictly better off?
options: No; that producer may be indifferent
Yes; every boundary rate gives strict gains
Yes; gains must be equal
No; both must be indifferent
repairQuestions.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
repairQuestions.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

repairSeedQuestions.q: Voluntary trade can benefit both sides when:
options: Each expects to gain from the exchange
One side is forced to trade
Prices are zero
All goods are identical
repairSeedQuestions.feedback: People voluntarily trade because each expects the exchange to make them better off.
repairSeedQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.

bridgeQuestions.q: A project lead is faster at every task but delegates data entry. Which concept explains the choice?
options: A price ceiling that limits payment for outsourced data entry
Absolute advantage because the lead is faster at data entry
Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead's time
Elimination of scarce time after the work is delegated
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Using absolute productivity instead of the opportunity cost of the lead's time.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Delegation can be efficient when the lead has a higher opportunity cost of doing data entry.

bridgeQuestions.q: A city can buy snowplow service from a neighboring county for less than the resources required to provide it internally. What does opportunity-cost reasoning suggest?
options: The city should remain self-sufficient even at a higher resource cost
The neighboring county cannot benefit from any voluntary contract
Money prices make the city's forgone alternatives irrelevant
Contracting can free city resources for other services
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Ignoring the internal resources forgone when the city provides the service itself.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Buying the service at lower opportunity cost frees scarce city resources for other uses.

bridgeQuestions.q: Scarcity forces two communities to choose how to use labor. Why can specialization help?
options: It directs labor toward lower-opportunity-cost tasks
It eliminates the underlying scarcity of labor.
It guarantees equal consumption
It makes workers equally productive
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a PPF help identify comparative advantage?
options: Its tradeoff reveals opportunity cost
Its size alone identifies advantage
It removes the need to compare alternatives
It proves every trade beneficial
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Computing or comparing the opportunity costs in the wrong direction.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Compute the forgone alternative per unit, then select the lower opportunity cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: Opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage. What does the basic model then predict about specialization?
options: Specialize in the lower-cost activity
Assign all tasks to the faster producer
Require equal gains before producing
Replace scarcity with self-sufficiency
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assigning every activity to the absolutely more productive producer.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: In the textbook model, specialization follows comparative advantage.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can terms of trade connect specialization to mutual gain?
options: A rate between costs can let both sides save resources
Any trading rate guarantees equal gains to both sides.
The rate erases tradeoffs
Only a boundary rate makes both better off
bridgeQuestions.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

elasticity.title: Elasticity
elasticity.description: Calculate and interpret price, income, cross-price, and supply elasticity; connect responsiveness to revenue, incidence, policy, trade, and business decisions.

objectiveLabels.ELAS.2: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand
objectiveLabels.ELAS.3: Connect demand elasticity to total revenue and marginal revenue
objectiveLabels.ELAS.4: Calculate and interpret price elasticity of supply
objectiveLabels.ELAS.5: Calculate and interpret income and cross-price elasticity
objectiveLabels.ELAS.6: Apply elasticity to taxes, policy, trade, and business decisions

easy.q: Economists use elasticity to measure:
options: How strongly one variable responds to a change in another
Only whether a variable rises or falls
The dollar value of every market transaction
The slope of any line without regard to units
easy.feedback: Elasticity is a responsiveness measure: percentage response divided by percentage change in a driver.

easy.q: Why is an elasticity coefficient usually unit-free?
options: It always uses dollars
It compares percentage changes
It divides quantity by price levels
It converts all values to index numbers
easy.feedback: Because both numerator and denominator are percentage changes, measurement units cancel.

easy.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1.8 is classified as:
options: Inelastic
Unit elastic
Elastic
Perfectly inelastic
easy.feedback: A demand elasticity greater than one means quantity responds proportionally more than price.

easy.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 0.45 is classified as:
options: Elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic
easy.feedback: A coefficient between zero and one is inelastic.

easy.q: A price elasticity of demand equal to 1 is:
options: Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Necessarily negative income elasticity
easy.feedback: Unit elasticity means equal proportional changes in price and quantity demanded.

easy.q: A vertical demand curve represents demand that is:
options: Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic everywhere
Elastic only at high prices
easy.feedback: Quantity does not respond to price on a vertical demand curve, so elasticity is zero.

easy.q: A horizontal demand curve represents demand that is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic everywhere
Perfectly elastic
Inelastic because slope is zero
easy.feedback: A tiny price increase eliminates quantity demanded along a perfectly elastic demand curve.

easy.q: Demand is generally more elastic when consumers have:
options: Fewer alternatives
Less time to adjust
A smaller share of income at stake
Many close substitutes
easy.feedback: Close substitutes make it easier to switch away when price rises.

easy.q: Compared with luxuries, necessities generally have demand that is:
options: Less elastic
More elastic
Perfectly elastic
Always unit elastic
easy.feedback: Consumers have less ability to reduce purchases of necessities after a price increase.

easy.q: Compared with a broadly defined market, a narrowly defined market usually has:
options: Less elastic demand
More elastic demand
The same elasticity by definition
Perfectly inelastic demand
easy.feedback: Narrow markets have more close substitutes, which raises demand elasticity.

easy.q: Demand tends to be more elastic for a good that takes up:
options: A tiny share of the buyer’s budget
No time to compare alternatives
A large share of the buyer’s budget
A fixed legal quantity
easy.feedback: Large budget shares give buyers a stronger reason to adjust.

easy.q: Over a longer time horizon, demand for gasoline is likely to become:
options: Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to available alternatives
More elastic
easy.feedback: Over time, drivers can change vehicles, locations, and travel habits.

easy.q: Which feature most directly makes demand for one brand of bottled water elastic?
options: Many nearly identical brands
Water is necessary for life
The product is sold in liters
The market price is positive
easy.feedback: Brand-level demand is elastic because buyers can switch among close substitutes.

easy.q: Which purchase is most likely to have inelastic demand in the short run?
options: A vacation package
A required medication with few substitutes
A premium restaurant meal
One brand of breakfast cereal
easy.feedback: Necessity, limited substitutes, and short adjustment time all reduce elasticity.

easy.q: Total revenue equals:
options: Price divided by quantity sold
Quantity sold minus price
Price multiplied by quantity sold
Elasticity multiplied by price
easy.feedback: Total revenue is P × Q.

easy.q: When demand is elastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
options: Rise
Remain unchanged
Become zero
Fall
easy.feedback: With elastic demand, the percentage drop in quantity is larger than the percentage price increase.

easy.q: When demand is inelastic, a price increase usually causes total revenue to:
options: Rise
Fall
Remain unchanged
Equal marginal revenue
easy.feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.

easy.q: When demand is unit elastic, a price change leaves total revenue:
options: Always higher
Approximately unchanged
Always lower
Equal to zero
easy.feedback: Equal proportional price and quantity changes offset in total revenue.

easy.q: Price elasticity of supply measures how quantity supplied responds to a change in:
options: Consumer income
The price of a complement in consumption
The good’s price
Buyer preferences
easy.feedback: Price elasticity of supply compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good’s price.

easy.q: Why is supply generally more elastic over a longer time horizon?
options: Less time to adjust production
No unused capacity
Inputs fixed by law
More time to adjust production
easy.feedback: A longer time horizon gives producers more time to expand capacity, change inputs, and otherwise adjust production.

easy.q: A firm with substantial unused capacity is likely to have short-run supply that is:
options: More elastic supply
Less elastic supply
Perfectly inelastic supply
No possible quantity change
easy.feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand.

easy.q: Which product is likely to have more elastic short-run supply?
options: Seats at tonight’s sold-out concert
A storable manufactured good
Fresh fish already caught today
Land in a fixed downtown block
easy.feedback: Storage and adjustable production make supply more responsive.

easy.q: A positive income elasticity usually identifies a:
options: Inferior good
Complement
Normal good
Perfectly inelastic good
easy.feedback: Demand for a normal good rises as income rises.

easy.q: A negative income elasticity usually identifies an:
options: Normal good
Substitute good
Unit-elastic good
Inferior good
easy.feedback: Demand for an inferior good falls as income rises.

easy.q: A positive cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both inferior
Both perfectly inelastic
easy.feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its substitute rises.

easy.q: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates that two goods are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both normal
Both elastic
easy.feedback: When the price of one rises, demand for its complement falls.

easy.q: A per-unit tax is generally borne more heavily by the side of the market that is:
options: More elastic
Legally required to mail the payment
Less elastic
Represented by the flatter curve in every case
easy.feedback: The less elastic side has fewer ways to avoid the taxed transaction.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. D2 is steeper than D1. Why isn’t slope alone a valid measure of elasticity?
options: Slope and elasticity measure the same response in the same units.
A negative slope makes demand inelastic at every point.
A steeper-looking curve has the same elasticity at every point.
Slope uses units; elasticity compares percentage changes.
easy.feedback: Slope measures units of price per unit of quantity and changes when axis units change. Elasticity measures percentage responsiveness; classification also depends on the price and quantity being compared.

easy.q: On the displayed linear demand curve, as you move downward from C through B toward A, price elasticity of demand generally:
options: Declines from elastic to unit elastic to inelastic
Remains constant because slope is constant
Rises from inelastic to elastic
Becomes zero immediately after B
easy.feedback: C lies in the elastic region, B is the unit-elastic midpoint, and A lies in the inelastic region.

easy.q: The midpoint method calculates percentage changes using:
options: Only the starting value
The average of the starting and ending values
Only the ending value
The larger value in both denominators
easy.feedback: Using averages makes the elasticity estimate symmetric for increases and decreases.

easy.q: At point B on the displayed linear demand curve, what price and quantity are shown?
options: $8 and 60 units
$12 and 30 units
$4 and 90 units
$8 and 90 units
easy.feedback: Point B is marked at P = $8 and Q = 60.

easy.q: Which labeled point is the midpoint of the displayed linear demand curve?
options: Point A
Point B
Point C
None of the labeled points
easy.feedback: The line runs from P = $16, Q = 0 to P = $0, Q = 120, so its midpoint is P = $8, Q = 60 at B.

easy.q: Which labeled point lies in the inelastic portion of the displayed linear demand curve?
options: Point B
Point C
Point A
All three points are equally elastic
easy.feedback: Below the midpoint of a linear demand curve, quantity is relatively large and price relatively small, so demand is inelastic; A is in that region.

easy.q: At a price of $10 in the displayed graph, which curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
options: D2, at 45 units
D1, at 35 units
D1, at 45 units
D2, at 55 units
easy.feedback: At P = $10, point B on D1 is Q = 45 while point D on D2 is Q = 35.

easy.q: When price is $6, which demand curve shows the larger quantity demanded?
options: D2, at 95 units
D1, at 55 units
D2, at 45 units
D1, at 95 units
easy.feedback: At P = $6, D1 is at point A with Q = 95, while D2 is at point C with Q = 55.

easy.q: A horizontal demand curve is the graphical form of:
options: Perfectly inelastic demand
Unit-elastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
A supply curve
easy.feedback: A horizontal demand curve is the limiting case of perfectly elastic demand.

easy.q: What elasticity case is represented by the vertical demand curve?
options: Perfectly elastic demand
Unit-elastic demand
A perfectly elastic supply curve
Perfectly inelastic demand
easy.feedback: A vertical demand curve means quantity demanded does not change when price changes.

easy.q: At a price of $8, what quantity is supplied on the short-run supply curve?
options: 60 units
100 units
70 units
40 units
easy.feedback: Point A on the short-run supply curve is Q = 70 at P = $8.

easy.q: Refer to the graph. Starting from P = $4 and Q = 60, which supply curve shows the larger increase in quantity supplied when price rises to $8?
options: Short-run supply
Both show the same response
Neither curve responds
Long-run supply
easy.feedback: Long-run supply reaches Q = 100, compared with Q = 70 in the short run.

easy.q: A bakery owns an unused oven and can add a second production shift quickly. Other things equal, its short-run supply is likely to be:
options: More elastic because output can expand without major new investment
More inelastic because unused capacity prevents adjustment
Perfectly inelastic because the bakery has fixed equipment
Unit elastic because capacity and price are unrelated
easy.feedback: Unused capacity makes it easier to raise output when price rises.

easy.q: Which situation generally makes supply more price elastic?
options: Production requires a fixed harvest already in the ground
All firms are operating at absolute capacity
The good must be supplied at one fixed quantity
Inputs can be moved easily into the industry
easy.feedback: Mobile inputs let producers expand or contract output more readily.

easy.q: A fresh strawberry farmer has only today to respond to a sudden price increase. Compared with supply over several growing seasons, today’s supply is usually:
options: Perfectly elastic
Exactly unit elastic
Less elastic
More elastic
easy.feedback: The very short run gives the farmer little time to change acreage, plants, or harvest capacity.

easy.q: A seller can store a product cheaply and release inventory when price rises. Cheap storage generally makes supply:
options: Unrelated to price
More elastic
Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
easy.feedback: Inventory can be shifted toward periods with higher prices, increasing quantity responsiveness.

easy.q: Household income rises and demand for bus rides falls. This pattern is most consistent with bus rides being:
options: A normal good with positive income elasticity
A luxury with income elasticity above one
A substitute good identified by cross-price elasticity
An inferior good for these consumers
easy.feedback: Demand moving opposite income implies negative income elasticity and an inferior good.

easy.q: Demand for restaurant meals rises when consumer income rises. The income elasticity of demand is therefore most likely:
options: Exactly zero by definition
A measure of supply responsiveness
Positive
Negative
easy.feedback: Normal goods have positive income elasticity because demand moves with income.

easy.q: If demand for a good changes very little when income changes, its income elasticity is likely to be:
options: The same as its price elasticity
Close to zero
Necessarily greater than one
Necessarily negative
easy.feedback: A small percentage demand response relative to income means an income elasticity near zero.

easy.q: The price of butter rises and demand for margarine rises. Butter and margarine are most likely:
options: Unrelated because cross-price effects cannot shift demand
Substitutes
Complements
Inferior goods
easy.feedback: Demand for one good moving in the same direction as the other good’s price implies positive cross-price elasticity.

easy.q: The price of game consoles falls and demand for compatible games rises. Consoles and games are most likely:
options: Complements
Substitutes
Both inferior goods
Goods with zero cross-price elasticity
easy.feedback: Demand for games moves opposite the console price, indicating negative cross-price elasticity.

easy.q: If a change in the price of one good has almost no effect on demand for another, their cross-price elasticity is probably:
options: Strongly positive
Strongly negative
Always equal to one
Near zero
easy.feedback: Little demand response to the other good’s price implies little economic relationship between the goods.

easy.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue rises. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to price
Elastic
easy.feedback: When demand is elastic, the percentage quantity increase outweighs the percentage price decrease, raising total revenue.

easy.q: A seller cuts price and total revenue falls. Over that price range, demand is most likely:
options: Perfectly elastic
Necessarily unit elastic
Inelastic
Elastic
easy.feedback: With inelastic demand, quantity rises proportionally less than price falls, so total revenue declines.

easy.q: If a price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged, demand over that range is closest to:
options: Income elastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Perfectly elastic
easy.feedback: At unit elasticity, the percentage price and quantity effects approximately offset.

easy.q: A firm sells 200 units at $15 each. Which expression gives total revenue?
easy.feedback: Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity sold.

easy.q: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is typically highest near the point where demand is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Most inelastic possible
Defined only by income elasticity
Unit elastic
easy.feedback: For a standard linear demand curve, total revenue reaches its maximum around unit elasticity.

easy.q: A price increase raises total revenue. Which demand condition is consistent with that result?
options: Demand must be perfectly elastic
Demand must have positive income elasticity
Demand is inelastic over the relevant range
Demand is elastic over the relevant range
easy.feedback: With inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the smaller quantity decline.

easy.q: If demand is much less elastic than supply, buyers usually bear:
options: None of the tax burden
Exactly half of every tax by rule
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
easy.feedback: The less elastic side of the market changes quantity less and bears more of the tax burden.

easy.q: If supply is much less elastic than demand, sellers usually bear:
options: Only the administrative cost of the tax
More of a per-unit tax burden
Less of a per-unit tax burden
None of the tax burden
easy.feedback: The less elastic side has fewer alternatives and bears more of the tax burden.

easy.q: A business facing highly elastic demand should be especially cautious about:
options: Raising price
Expanding output
Tracking competitors
Estimating variable cost
easy.feedback: With elastic demand, a price increase can cause a proportionally larger loss of quantity demanded.

easy.q: A business facing very inelastic demand can raise price with a relatively small percentage decline in:
options: Fixed cost
Supply elasticity
Producer technology
Quantity demanded
easy.feedback: Inelastic demand means quantity demanded responds proportionally less than price.

easy.q: Other things equal, a tax reduces the quantity traded by more when demand and supply are:
options: Perfectly vertical
Unrelated to price
More elastic
More inelastic
easy.feedback: More responsive buyers and sellers reduce traded quantity more when a tax wedge is introduced.

easy.q: A policy that raises price will reduce consumption most strongly when demand is:
options: Independent of price
More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
easy.feedback: Elastic demand produces a larger percentage quantity response to a given percentage price change.

easy.q: An export industry can expand output more after a world-price increase when its supply is:
options: More elastic
More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Measured only by income elasticity
easy.feedback: More elastic supply allows producers to respond more strongly to the higher price.

easy.q: If employers can easily substitute machines for a type of labor when wages rise, demand for that labor is likely to be:
options: More inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unrelated to substitution possibilities
More elastic
easy.feedback: Availability of substitutes makes factor demand more responsive to its price.

easy.q: A city wants a fee to sharply reduce use of a service. The fee is more likely to change behavior when demand for the service is:
options: Perfectly inelastic
Vertical at every price
Elastic
Inelastic
easy.feedback: Elastic demand means usage responds strongly to a price-like charge.

medium.q: A commuter has few alternatives this week but can relocate or change vehicles over several years. Demand for gasoline is likely to be:
options: More elastic in the short run than in the long run
Equally elastic in both periods by definition
More elastic in the long run than in the short run
Perfectly elastic in both periods
medium.feedback: Longer adjustment periods create more substitution possibilities.

medium.q: Demand for “food” is less elastic than demand for “restaurant lunches” mainly because:
options: Restaurant lunches are always necessities
Food has a steeper curve in every graph
Broad markets always have lower prices
Food is a broader market with fewer substitutes outside the category
medium.feedback: Narrower definitions expose more alternatives within the broader category.

medium.q: A streaming service raises price by 5 percent and subscriptions fall by 12 percent. Demand is:
options: Elastic
Inelastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly inelastic
medium.feedback: Quantity changes proportionally more than price, so elasticity exceeds one.

medium.q: A clinic raises a required treatment price by 8 percent and visits fall by 2 percent. Demand is:
options: Elastic
Inelastic
Unit elastic
Perfectly elastic
medium.feedback: Quantity changes proportionally less than price.

medium.q: A theater cuts ticket price and total revenue rises. This reveals that demand over that range is:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Elastic
Necessarily unit elastic
medium.feedback: A price cut raises revenue only when quantity responds more than proportionally.

medium.q: A toll road raises its fee and total revenue also rises. Demand over that range is most likely:
options: Elastic
Perfectly elastic
Negative income elastic
Inelastic
medium.feedback: Revenue moving with price indicates inelastic demand.

medium.q: A seller operating where demand is elastic lowers price. Which result is most likely?
options: Quantity rises by a larger percentage than price falls
Quantity rises by a smaller percentage than price falls
Quantity does not change
Total revenue must fall
medium.feedback: Elastic demand means a proportionally larger quantity response.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. As you move down the linear demand curve from C through B toward A, price elasticity of demand generally:
options: Increase
Decline
Remain constant
Switch immediately from zero to infinity
medium.feedback: The price-to-quantity ratio falls as movement continues down the line, so elasticity declines.

medium.q: At the midpoint of a linear demand curve, demand is typically:
options: Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic
Income inelastic
medium.feedback: For a linear demand curve, the midpoint separates elastic and inelastic regions.

medium.q: A firm raises price while operating on the elastic portion of its demand curve. Total revenue will:
options: Increase
Stay constant
Equal total cost
Decrease
medium.feedback: The percentage quantity loss exceeds the percentage price gain.

medium.q: Why might a seller avoid operating on the inelastic portion of a demand curve when marginal cost is positive?
options: Raising price would increase revenue and reduce quantity-related cost
Cutting price would increase both revenue and profit automatically
Marginal revenue is positive there
