Demand becomes perfectly elastic there
medium.feedback: On the inelastic region, a price increase raises revenue while fewer units are produced.

medium.q: Marginal revenue is positive when demand is:
options: Inelastic
Elastic
Perfectly inelastic
At the quantity intercept
medium.feedback: Selling another unit raises total revenue on the elastic portion.

medium.q: Marginal revenue equals zero where demand is:
options: Perfectly elastic
Perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic
Income elastic
medium.feedback: Total revenue is maximized and locally unchanged at unit elasticity.

medium.q: A farmer cannot change this season’s planted acreage after a price increase. Short-run supply is likely:
options: Relatively elastic
Perfectly elastic
Unrelated to production constraints
Relatively inelastic
medium.feedback: Fixed acreage and biological lags limit immediate output response.

medium.q: Housing supply is typically more elastic in a growing suburb than in a fully built downtown because the suburb has:
options: More available land and expansion capacity
More inelastic demand
A necessarily higher price level
No construction time
medium.feedback: Available land and development capacity make quantity more responsive.

medium.q: Supply of seats for tonight’s concert is:
options: Highly elastic
Nearly perfectly inelastic
Unit elastic by definition
Perfectly elastic after the show starts
medium.feedback: The number of seats cannot expand for that event.

medium.q: An income elasticity of 1.6 suggests the good is:
options: An inferior good
A complement
A normal good whose demand is income elastic
A normal good whose demand is income inelastic
medium.feedback: Positive income elasticity above one is often associated with a luxury-type normal good.

medium.q: An income elasticity of 0.4 suggests the good is:
options: An inferior good
A substitute
A normal good whose demand falls as income rises
A normal good whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
medium.feedback: The positive sign indicates normal; magnitude below one indicates income inelasticity.

medium.q: A cross-price elasticity of 0.8 between tea and coffee implies they are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both inferior
Unrelated because the value is below one
medium.feedback: A positive cross-price coefficient indicates substitutes; magnitude measures strength.

medium.q: A cross-price elasticity of −0.6 between printers and ink cartridges implies they are:
options: Substitutes
Complements
Both normal goods
Perfectly inelastic
medium.feedback: A negative cross-price coefficient means demand moves opposite the other good’s price.

medium.q: Demand is very inelastic and supply is relatively elastic. Which side of the market will bear most of a new excise tax?
options: Sellers
The government
Buyers
Whichever side writes the check
medium.feedback: Buyers have fewer ways to avoid the taxed market.

medium.q: Demand is relatively elastic and supply is very inelastic. Which side of the market will bear most of a new tax?
options: Buyers
Consumers and producers exactly equally
The side named in the statute
Sellers
medium.feedback: Sellers are the less elastic side and bear more burden.

medium.q: Which tax is most likely to create a relatively small reduction in traded quantity?
options: A tax in a market where both demand and supply are inelastic
A tax where both sides are highly elastic
A tax on a market with many substitutes and mobile producers
Any tax legally collected from sellers
medium.feedback: Inelastic quantities respond less, so fewer mutually beneficial trades disappear.

medium.q: A hotel expects convention visitors to have less elastic demand than vacation travelers. If the hotel is focused on revenue, what pricing pattern is most consistent with that difference in elasticity?
options: A lower price for convention visitors because their demand is less elastic
A higher price for convention visitors when lawful and feasible
The same price because elasticity never affects pricing
A zero price for vacation travelers
medium.feedback: Groups with less elastic demand can sustain higher markups.

medium.q: A city wants a congestion toll to reduce peak-hour trips substantially. The policy is more effective when trip demand is:
options: Inelastic
Perfectly inelastic
Elastic
Unit-free
medium.feedback: An elastic quantity response produces a larger behavioral change.

medium.q: A city wants a cigarette tax primarily to raise stable revenue rather than sharply reduce smoking. That goal is aided by:
options: Elastic demand
Perfectly elastic supply
A positive cross-price elasticity with all goods
Inelastic demand
medium.feedback: Inelastic demand preserves the tax base after price rises.

medium.q: A drought reduces farm output, causing price to rise sharply while farmers’ total revenue rises. This pattern is consistent with:
options: Inelastic demand for the crop
Elastic demand for the crop
Perfectly elastic crop supply
Unit income elasticity
medium.feedback: A supply reduction raises price; with inelastic demand, the price effect dominates the quantity loss.

medium.q: The displayed linear demand curve has constant slope, yet elasticity changes along it. Which statement correctly compares slope and elasticity?
options: Slope and elasticity are both constant everywhere on a linear demand curve
Slope is constant on a linear demand curve, but elasticity usually changes along it
Elasticity is constant on a linear demand curve, but slope usually changes along it
Slope and elasticity both change only when a demand curve is nonlinear
medium.feedback: Elasticity also depends on the price and quantity at the point.

medium.q: Why is the midpoint method preferred when comparing two price-quantity observations?
options: It always produces an elasticity of one
It removes the need for percentage changes
It gives one symmetric estimate in either direction
It uses only the lower price and quantity
medium.feedback: Average denominators eliminate direction-dependent base values.

medium.q: A price increase reduces quantity demanded, so the raw price elasticity of demand is negative. Economists usually report:
options: Its square
Only the negative sign
Zero whenever price and quantity move oppositely
Its absolute value
medium.feedback: Demand elasticity is usually stated as a positive magnitude for classification.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at point C?
medium.feedback: At C, P = $12 and Q = 30, so total revenue is $12 × 30 = $360.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is total revenue at point B?
medium.feedback: At B, P = $8 and Q = 60, so total revenue is $480.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Compare points C and B and calculate total revenue at each. What does the change imply about demand over that interval?
options: Demand is inelastic
Demand is elastic
Demand is perfectly inelastic
Demand is unit elastic throughout the interval
medium.feedback: When a price cut raises total revenue, demand is elastic over the interval.

medium.q: On D1, compare the labeled quantities at the two marked prices. What is the change in quantity demanded?
options: 50 units
20 units
40 units
60 units
medium.feedback: The change is 95 − 45 = 50 units.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. How much does quantity demanded change between the two marked points on D2?
options: 50 units
20 units
35 units
90 units
medium.feedback: The change is 55 − 35 = 20 units.

medium.q: For a price decrease from $10 to $6 on the displayed demand curves, which curve is more price elastic over the labeled interval?
options: D2
They have identical elasticity
D1
Elasticity cannot be compared from the labeled points
medium.feedback: D1 has the much larger proportional quantity response to the same proportional price change.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. As price changes between the two labeled points on vertical D2, what happens to quantity demanded?
options: It remains 50 units
It rises to 70 units
It falls to 30 units
It becomes zero
medium.feedback: D2 is vertical at Q = 50, so the price change does not alter quantity demanded.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. When price rises from $4 to $8, how much does quantity supplied rise in the short run?
options: 10 units
40 units
30 units
70 units
medium.feedback: Short-run quantity rises from 60 to 70, a 10-unit increase.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Compare the short-run and long-run supply responses to the same price change. Why is the long-run response larger?
options: Producers have less time to change output over the shown interval
Producers have more time to adjust capacity and inputs
Long-run quantity is fixed by definition
Price changes are smaller in the long run
medium.feedback: More adjustment time usually allows firms to expand capacity, enter, switch inputs, and otherwise respond more strongly.

medium.q: Firm A can add workers and rent extra machines within a month. Firm B needs two years to build a new plant. For the same one-month price increase, whose supply should be more elastic?
options: Firm A’s, because it can adjust capacity sooner
Firm B’s, because long construction times create flexibility
Both equally, because price changes determine elasticity by themselves
Neither, because supply elasticity applies only to agriculture
medium.feedback: Faster capacity adjustment makes quantity supplied more responsive in the relevant time period.

medium.q: A concert venue has 20,000 fixed seats for tonight but can schedule additional shows next month. Supply of seats is likely to be:
options: More elastic tonight than next month
Equally elastic in both periods
Perfectly elastic tonight and perfectly inelastic next month
More inelastic tonight than next month
medium.feedback: Tonight’s capacity is fixed, while a longer horizon permits additional performances.

medium.q: Two firms face the same price increase. One has idle machinery; the other is already using every machine around the clock. Which response is most likely?
options: Both must have the same percentage increase in output
Neither can change output because price does not affect supply
The firm with idle machinery has the larger percentage increase in output
The capacity-constrained firm has the larger percentage increase in output
medium.feedback: Unused capacity makes output easier to expand, increasing supply elasticity.

medium.q: Suppose lumber producers can quickly redirect logs among several mills, while a specialized chemical plant requires dedicated equipment. Other things equal, supply should be:
options: Perfectly inelastic in both industries in every time period
More elastic for lumber because inputs are easier to reallocate
More elastic for the chemical because specialized equipment raises flexibility
Equally elastic because both industries sell physical goods
medium.feedback: Ease of reallocating inputs is a major determinant of supply responsiveness.

medium.q: A 10% increase in price causes quantity supplied to rise by only 3%. What does that imply about supply?
options: Supply is inelastic over the measured range
Supply is elastic over the measured range
Supply is unit elastic over the measured range
Supply is perfectly elastic over the measured range
medium.feedback: A percentage quantity response smaller than the percentage price change gives PES below one.

medium.q: A good has income elasticity of 0.35. Which description fits best?
options: A normal necessity whose demand rises less than proportionally with income
An inferior good whose demand falls as income rises
A luxury whose demand rises more than proportionally with income
A substitute whose demand responds to another good’s price
medium.feedback: Positive income elasticity below one is commonly associated with necessities.

medium.q: Income rises 8% and quantity demanded for a service rises 12%. Based on these changes, the service is best classified as:
options: An inferior good
A normal necessity with elasticity below one
A complement identified by cross-price elasticity
A normal luxury
medium.feedback: Demand rises more than proportionally with income, so income elasticity exceeds one.

medium.q: A retailer estimates income elasticity for its store brand at -0.6. During a strong income expansion, the retailer should expect demand for the store brand to:
options: Remain fixed because elasticity is negative
Move only if the store changes its own price
Fall, other things equal
Rise more than income
medium.feedback: Negative income elasticity indicates an inferior good, so higher income reduces demand.

medium.q: Cross-price elasticity between streaming service A and streaming service B is +1.3. What is the best interpretation?
options: They are unrelated because only the sign of price elasticity matters
They are inferior goods because the coefficient is positive
They are substitutes and demand for one is fairly responsive to the other’s price
They are complements because the coefficient is greater than one
medium.feedback: A positive cross-price elasticity signals substitutes; the magnitude indicates a meaningful response.

medium.q: Cross-price elasticity between printers and ink cartridges is -0.7. If printer prices rise, demand for ink cartridges should generally:
options: Become perfectly elastic
Fall
Rise
Stay unchanged by definition
medium.feedback: A negative cross-price elasticity indicates complements, so higher printer prices reduce demand for ink.

medium.q: The price of tea rises 5% and demand for coffee rises 2%. Which conclusion is best?
options: Coffee and tea are substitutes with a positive cross-price elasticity
Coffee and tea are complements with a negative cross-price elasticity
Coffee is inferior because its demand increased
Tea supply is elastic because coffee demand changed
medium.feedback: The demand response is in the same direction as the other good’s price change, so cross-price elasticity is positive.

medium.q: Demand elasticity is 0.3 and supply elasticity is 1.4. Which side is likely to bear more of a new per-unit tax?
options: The government, because elasticities determine revenue only
Buyers, because demand is less elastic
Sellers, because supply is more elastic
Both exactly equally
medium.feedback: The demand side is less responsive and therefore bears more of the tax burden.

medium.q: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.1. If its only goal is to raise total revenue and demand does not shift, which price move is more promising?
options: A price decrease
A price increase
No price can affect revenue
A higher fixed cost
medium.feedback: Elastic demand means a price cut can raise total revenue through a more-than-proportional quantity increase.

medium.q: Two markets face the same tax. Market A has very elastic demand and supply; Market B has very inelastic demand and supply. Which market should experience the larger reduction in quantity traded?
options: Market B
Both must have the same quantity change
Neither market changes quantity under a tax
Market A
medium.feedback: More elastic buyers and sellers respond more strongly to the tax-created price wedge.

medium.q: A conservation surcharge is intended to reduce water use. Which condition makes the surcharge least effective at changing quantity demanded in the short run?
options: Many close substitutes for water use
A long adjustment horizon
Very inelastic water demand
Very elastic water demand
medium.feedback: When demand is very inelastic, quantity responds little to the higher effective price.

hard.q: A tool-rental shop compares two weekly rates. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $30 to $36 and quantity demanded from 400 to 360. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 0.58, inelastic; use $36 to earn $960 more.
About 0.58, inelastic; use $30 to earn $960 more.
About 1.73, elastic; use $30 to earn $960 more.
About 0.58, elastic; both prices earn the same revenue.
hard.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(360 - 400) / ((360 + 400) / 2)| divided by |(36 - 30) / ((36 + 30) / 2)|, about 0.58. Revenue is $12,000 at $30 and $12,960 at $36. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for specialty coffee subscriptions changes from $18 to $21 and quantity demanded changes from 800 to 680. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.05, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for museum admissions changes from $14 to $11 and quantity demanded changes from 500 to 650. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.09, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: A print service tests two poster prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $25 to $30 and quantity demanded from 480 to 360. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 1.57, elastic; use $30 to earn $1,200 more.
About 0.64, inelastic; use $30 to earn $1,200 more.
About 1.57, inelastic; both prices earn $12,000.
About 1.57, elastic; use $25 to earn $1,200 more.
hard.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(360 - 480) / ((360 + 480) / 2)| divided by |(30 - 25) / ((30 + 25) / 2)|, about 1.57. Revenue is $12,000 at $25 and $10,800 at $30. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for fitness memberships changes from $35 to $40 and quantity demanded changes from 900 to 765. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.22, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for festival tickets changes from $50 to $44 and quantity demanded changes from 600 to 720. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.42, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for meal-kit subscriptions changes from $60 to $66 and quantity demanded changes from 1000 to 850. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.7, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for airport parking days changes from $16 to $20 and quantity demanded changes from 1500 to 1170. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.11, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of a professional exam-prep course falls from $250 to $225, and quantity demanded rises from 400 seats to 480 seats. What is the price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 1.73, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, price for premium headphones changes from $180 to $198 and quantity demanded changes from 700 to 560. What is price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint percentage change in quantity divided by the midpoint percentage change in price is about 2.33, so demand is elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of artisan bread loaves changes from $4 to $5 and quantity supplied changes from 900 to 1080. What is price elasticity of supply?
hard.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.82, classified as inelastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of rental bicycles changes from $12 to $15 and quantity supplied changes from 300 to 390. What is price elasticity of supply?
hard.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.17, classified as elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of greenhouse tomatoes changes from $3 to $4 and quantity supplied changes from 1000 to 1180. What is price elasticity of supply?
hard.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.58, classified as inelastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of cloud-server capacity rises from $40 to $50 per unit, and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 700 units. What is the price elasticity of supply?
hard.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 1.5, classified as elastic.

hard.q: Using the midpoint method, the price of hotel rooms rises from $150 to $180, and short-run quantity supplied rises from 800 to 840 rooms. What is the price elasticity of supply?
hard.feedback: The midpoint calculation gives a supply elasticity of about 0.27, classified as inelastic.

hard.q: The displayed linear demand curve has constant slope. Why can the upper portion near C be elastic while the lower portion near A is inelastic?
options: The slope changes sign at the midpoint
Consumers become irrational below the midpoint
Price and quantity move in the same direction on the lower portion
Percentage bases differ along the curve despite constant slope
hard.feedback: Elasticity compares percentage changes, so the price-quantity location matters even when slope is constant.

hard.q: A seller cuts price by 8 percent and quantity demanded rises by 5 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Demand is inelastic and total revenue falls
Demand is elastic and total revenue rises
Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
Demand is perfectly inelastic and quantity cannot change
hard.feedback: Elasticity is about 0.625. With inelastic demand, a price cut reduces total revenue.

hard.q: A seller raises price by 6 percent and quantity demanded falls by 15 percent. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Demand is inelastic and total revenue rises
Demand is elastic and total revenue falls
Demand is unit elastic and total revenue is unchanged
Demand is income elastic
hard.feedback: Elasticity is 2.5, so the proportionally larger quantity loss reduces revenue.

hard.q: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 2.5. Holding other factors constant, a 4 percent price cut is predicted to change quantity demanded by approximately:
options: A 1.6 percent increase
A 6.5 percent decrease
A 10 percent increase
A 10 percent decrease
hard.feedback: Quantity response is elasticity times the price change magnitude: 2.5 × 4% = 10%.

hard.q: A firm estimates demand elasticity at 0.3. A 10 percent price increase is predicted to reduce quantity demanded by approximately:
options: 30 percent
13 percent
0.3 percent
3 percent
hard.feedback: The predicted quantity response is 0.3 × 10% = 3%.

hard.q: A public transit agency faces inelastic peak demand but elastic off-peak demand. Which pricing strategy is most consistent with revenue management?
options: Raise peak fares and use discounts to attract off-peak riders
Cut peak fares and raise off-peak fares
Charge zero in both periods
Ignore elasticity because both services use the same buses
hard.feedback: Higher prices fit the less elastic segment, while discounts can expand the more elastic segment.

hard.q: A product has many substitutes, but buyers have signed one-year contracts. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Demand must be perfectly elastic immediately
Short-run demand can be inelastic; renewal demand more elastic
Contracts make long-run demand less elastic
Substitutes matter only for supply elasticity
hard.feedback: Contractual switching costs suppress short-run response but not necessarily later response.

hard.q: A tax is imposed in a market with perfectly inelastic demand and upward-sloping supply. Who bears the economic burden?
options: Sellers bear the entire tax
The burden is necessarily split equally
Buyers bear the entire tax
The government bears the tax
hard.feedback: Buyers cannot change quantity, so the consumer price rises by the full tax.

hard.q: A tax is imposed in a market with perfectly inelastic supply and downward-sloping demand. Who bears the economic burden?
options: Buyers bear the entire tax
The burden is necessarily split equally
No one bears the tax because quantity is fixed
Sellers bear the entire tax
hard.feedback: Suppliers cannot withdraw quantity, so the net price they receive falls by the full tax.

hard.q: Two markets generate the same tax revenue. Market A has more elastic demand and supply than Market B. Which market likely loses more mutually beneficial trades?
options: Market A
Market B
Both necessarily lose the same number
The statutory payer determines the loss
hard.feedback: More elastic quantities respond more strongly to the wedge, increasing the reduction in trade.

hard.q: A positive income elasticity of 2.2 for international vacations means that a recession is likely to cause demand to:
options: Rise because vacations are inferior
Fall more than proportionally to income
Remain unchanged because the coefficient is positive
Fall less than proportionally to income
hard.feedback: A positive coefficient above one identifies an income-elastic normal good.

hard.q: A cross-price elasticity between ride-share trips and subway rides is 0.2. Which inference is safest?
options: They are strong complements
They are unrelated because 0.2 is below one
They are weak substitutes in the observed range
Both are inferior goods
hard.feedback: The positive sign indicates substitutes; the small magnitude indicates a weak relationship.

hard.q: A cross-price elasticity between game consoles and compatible games is −1.4. Which inference is safest?
options: They are substitutes because the magnitude exceeds one
The console is an inferior good
Demand for games is perfectly inelastic
They are relatively strong complements
hard.feedback: The negative sign indicates complements, and the magnitude suggests a strong link.

hard.q: A price floor creates a surplus. All else equal, which supply characteristic would make the surplus larger for a given increase in price?
options: More elastic supply
More inelastic supply
Perfectly inelastic demand alone
A smaller number of sellers by itself
hard.feedback: More elastic suppliers expand quantity supplied more in response to the supported price.

hard.q: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage. Which demand characteristic makes quantity demanded rise more sharply at the controlled price?
options: More inelastic demand
More elastic demand
Perfectly inelastic supply
A larger tax wedge
hard.feedback: More elastic demand responds more to the lower controlled price.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Using points C and B and midpoint percentages, which elasticity and revenue implication describe a move from C to B?
options: About 1.67, elastic; the price cut lowers total revenue.
About 0.60, inelastic; the price cut raises total revenue.
About 1.67, elastic; the price cut raises total revenue.
About 1.00, unit elastic; total revenue is unchanged.
hard.feedback: C is P = 12, Q = 30 and B is P = 8, Q = 60. Midpoint elasticity is (30/45)/(4/10) = 1.67. Revenue rises from 360 to 480, so the elastic interval supports the price cut.

hard.q: For the B-to-A interval, calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand from the graph.
hard.feedback: The percentage quantity change is 30/75 = 40% and the percentage price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving elasticity about 0.60.

hard.q: Across the full C-to-A interval, what midpoint price elasticity does the graph imply?
hard.feedback: From C to A, quantity changes by 60 around an average of 60 and price changes by 8 around an average of 8, so both percentage changes are 100%.

hard.q: Why does elasticity change along the displayed linear demand curve even though the curve has constant slope?
options: The demand curve changes slope at B
The price-to-quantity ratio changes along the curve
Elasticity ignores percentage changes over the shown interval
Quantity becomes fixed below B
hard.feedback: For a linear demand curve, point elasticity depends on both the constant slope term and the changing P/Q ratio.

hard.q: Using the two labeled points on D1, what is the midpoint price elasticity of demand?
hard.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 50/70 ≈ 71.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 1.43.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. What is the midpoint price elasticity of demand between the marked points on D2?
hard.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 20/45 ≈ 44.4% and the price change is 4/8 = 50%, so elasticity is about 0.89.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Using the labeled $10-to-$6 price change, which classification is correct?
options: Both D1 and D2 are elastic
D1 is elastic and D2 is inelastic
D1 is inelastic and D2 is elastic
Both D1 and D2 are unit elastic
hard.feedback: The midpoint coefficients are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2.

hard.q: The price elasticity coefficient of a perfectly inelastic demand curve is:
options: Infinity
hard.feedback: With zero percentage change in quantity despite a price change, the elasticity coefficient is zero.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Using the common starting point and point A on the short-run supply curve, calculate the midpoint price elasticity of supply.
hard.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 10/65 ≈ 15.4% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.23.

hard.q: A garden workshop compares admission prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $40 to $48 and quantity demanded from 150 to 135. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 0.58, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
About 0.58, inelastic; $48 raises revenue by $480.
About 1.73, elastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
About 0.58, inelastic; $40 raises revenue by $480.
hard.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(135 - 150) / ((135 + 150) / 2)| divided by |(48 - 40) / ((48 + 40) / 2)|, about 0.58. Revenue is $6,000 at $40 and $6,480 at $48. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

hard.q: A digital lesson service compares subscription prices. Holding demand conditions fixed, price changes from $9 to $12 and quantity demanded from 900 to 600. Using midpoint elasticity in absolute value, which calculation and revenue decision are supported for these two prices?
options: About 1.40, elastic; $9 earns $900 more than $12.
About 1.40, elastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
About 0.71, inelastic; $12 earns $900 more than $9.
About 1.40, unit elastic; the prices earn equal revenue.
hard.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is |(600 - 900) / ((600 + 900) / 2)| divided by |(12 - 9) / ((12 + 9) / 2)|, about 1.4. Revenue is $8,100 at $9 and $7,200 at $12. Compare these feasible prices; the interval does not establish a global optimum.

hard.q: A repair service can charge $50 for 120 jobs or $45 for 140 jobs, with enough capacity for either. Holding other demand factors fixed, use midpoint elasticity to choose the higher-revenue price.
options: About 1.46, elastic; choose $50 because elastic demand favors a higher price.
About 0.68, inelastic; choose $50 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
About 1.00, unit elastic; choose either because the revenues are equal.
About 1.46, elastic; choose $45 because revenue is $6,300 rather than $6,000.
hard.feedback: The midpoint changes are 20/130 for quantity and 5/47.5 for price, giving about 1.46. Revenue is 45 × 140 = $6,300 versus 50 × 120 = $6,000. The price cut raises revenue over this interval.

hard.q: A tax is imposed in a market with very inelastic demand and very elastic supply. Which combination is most likely?
options: Consumers bear little of the tax and quantity rises
Consumers bear most of the tax and quantity falls relatively little
Producers bear most of the tax and quantity falls sharply
The burden is split equally and quantity cannot change
hard.feedback: The less elastic demand side bears more burden, while limited quantity responsiveness restrains the decline in trade.

hard.q: A regulator compares two markets facing identical per-unit fees. In Market X, demand and supply are relatively inelastic; in Market Y, both are relatively elastic. Which claim is best?
options: Market Y is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Market X is likely to have the larger quantity reduction and larger efficiency loss
Both markets must have identical quantity reductions because the fee is identical
Elasticity affects tax incidence but never deadweight loss
hard.feedback: Flatter, more elastic curves generate stronger behavioral responses and typically more lost trades.

hard.q: A firm sells a product with few substitutes today, but several close substitutes will enter next year. Holding other factors constant, what should happen to the firm’s pricing power over time?
options: It should strengthen as demand becomes more inelastic
It should be unchanged because substitutes do not affect elasticity
It should disappear only if supply becomes perfectly elastic
It should weaken as demand becomes more elastic
hard.feedback: More close substitutes make customers more responsive to the firm’s price.

hard.q: A subsidy lowers the effective price of a product. Policymakers want a large increase in quantity consumed rather than mainly a transfer to existing buyers. Which market is the better candidate?
options: A market with perfectly vertical demand
Elasticity is irrelevant to quantity response
A market with more elastic demand
A market with more inelastic demand
hard.feedback: More elastic demand produces a larger quantity response to the lower effective price.

elite.q: A market researcher observes annual software licenses: price moves from $80 to $92, while quantity demanded moves from 5000 to 4100. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.42; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes stadium club seats: price moves from $300 to $345, while quantity demanded moves from 900 to 720. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.59; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes specialty insulin pumps: price moves from $5000 to $5400, while quantity demanded moves from 1200 to 1140. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 0.67; this places the observation in the inelastic range.

elite.q: A ceramics studio has this unchanged demand schedule: $32 for 180 sessions, $40 for 160, and $48 for 110. It currently charges $40 and can serve all scheduled buyers. Which recommendation follows from midpoint elasticity and revenue across the two adjacent intervals?
options: Choose $32: the lower interval is elastic, so the additional sessions raise revenue.
Keep $40: the lower interval is inelastic and the upper interval is elastic, so either listed change lowers revenue.
Choose $48: the upper interval is inelastic, so the higher price raises revenue.
Choose either alternative: equal $8 changes produce equal revenue gains.
elite.feedback: For $32–$40, midpoint elasticity is (20/170)/(8/36) ≈ 0.53. For $40–$48 it is (50/135)/(8/44) ≈ 2.04. Revenues are $5,760, $6,400, and $5,280; $40 is best among the three quoted prices.

elite.q: A market researcher observes organic grocery boxes: price moves from $45 to $51, while quantity demanded moves from 1600 to 1360. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.3; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes private tutoring hours: price moves from $60 to $72, while quantity demanded moves from 1000 to 760. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.5; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes winter heating fuel: price moves from $3.2 to $3.8, while quantity demanded moves from 8000 to 7400. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 0.45; this places the observation in the inelastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes luxury handbags: price moves from $900 to $810, while quantity demanded moves from 450 to 585. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 2.48; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes online news subscriptions: price moves from $12 to $15, while quantity demanded moves from 10000 to 7600. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.23; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A market researcher observes commercial drone rentals: price moves from $200 to $230, while quantity demanded moves from 700 to 560. Use the midpoint method to estimate elasticity and select the coefficient.
elite.feedback: The midpoint estimate is about 1.59; this places the observation in the elastic range.

elite.q: A monopolist currently operates where demand elasticity is 0.7 and marginal cost is positive. Which adjustment is most likely to increase profit?
options: Raise price and reduce output
Lower price and expand output
Hold output because marginal revenue is positive
Move farther into the inelastic region
elite.feedback: In the inelastic region, marginal revenue is negative; raising price increases revenue and reduces cost.

elite.q: A firm estimates elasticity using percentage changes from the original value and gets 1.20 for a price increase but 0.83 for the reverse price decrease. What caused the discrepancy?
options: Demand changed from elastic to inelastic solely because direction reversed
Different base values; the midpoint method would produce one symmetric estimate
Elasticity cannot be measured between two points
The correct method always uses the larger endpoint
elite.feedback: Conventional percentage changes depend on the chosen base, while midpoint percentages do not.

elite.q: A linear demand curve intersects the price axis at $100 and the quantity axis at 1,000 units. Near the price intercept, which combination of elasticity and marginal revenue is expected?
options: Inelastic demand and negative marginal revenue
Unit-elastic demand and zero price
Elastic demand and positive marginal revenue
Perfectly inelastic demand and maximum quantity
elite.feedback: Upper portions of a linear demand curve are elastic, where marginal revenue is positive.

elite.q: A linear demand curve intersects the axes. At a point near the quantity intercept, which combination is expected?
options: Elastic demand and positive marginal revenue
Unit-elastic demand and maximum price
Perfectly elastic demand and zero quantity
Inelastic demand and negative marginal revenue
elite.feedback: Lower portions are inelastic and adding sales reduces total revenue.

elite.q: A tour operator can serve all customers at either quoted price: $24 attracts 250 buyers and $20 attracts 320. Other demand conditions are fixed. Which midpoint estimate and revenue advice follow?
options: About 1.35, elastic; use $20, which raises revenue by $400.
About 1.35, elastic; use $24, which raises revenue by $400.
About 0.74, inelastic; use $24, which raises revenue by $400.
About 1.00, unit elastic; the two prices earn the same revenue.
elite.feedback: Midpoint elasticity is (70/285)/(4/22) ≈ 1.35. The lower price earns 20 × 320 = $6,400 instead of 24 × 250 = $6,000. The larger proportional quantity response offsets the price cut.

elite.q: A firm sells 2,000 units at $15. After raising price to $17, it sells 1,700 units. Which statement is correct?
options: Total revenue rises, indicating inelastic demand
Total revenue falls from $30,000 to $28,900, indicating elastic demand over the range
Revenue is unchanged, indicating unit elasticity
The change reveals income elasticity
elite.feedback: Revenue falls when price rises, so quantity responded strongly enough to indicate elastic demand.

elite.q: A government taxes a product with inelastic demand partly to raise revenue. Which additional fact most threatens the stability of that revenue over time?
options: The product currently takes a small budget share
Supply is upward sloping
Close substitutes are developing rapidly
The statute requires sellers to remit the tax
elite.feedback: New substitutes can make long-run demand substantially more elastic.

elite.q: A carbon tax is intended to reduce emissions. Which market configuration creates the strongest quantity response to a given tax wedge?
options: Perfectly inelastic demand and supply
Inelastic demand with fixed supply
The legal obligation placed on firms
Relatively elastic demand and relatively elastic supply
elite.feedback: Greater responsiveness on both sides produces a larger reduction in equilibrium quantity.

elite.q: A subsidy is introduced in a market with inelastic demand and elastic supply. Who captures most of the benefit?
options: Buyers through a lower price
Sellers through a higher net price
The side that files the subsidy paperwork
Benefits must split equally
elite.feedback: The less elastic side captures more of a subsidy just as it bears more of a tax.

elite.q: A price ceiling lowers rent. In a city where long-run housing supply is much more elastic than short-run supply, how is the housing shortage likely to change over time?
options: Smaller because supply becomes more responsive
Larger because suppliers reduce quantity more over time
Unchanged because the ceiling is fixed
Zero because elasticity eliminates controls
elite.feedback: More elastic long-run supply creates a larger quantity-supplied response to the lower controlled price.

elite.q: An agricultural innovation makes crop supply more elastic. After a demand increase, compared with the old supply curve, equilibrium will show:
options: A smaller quantity increase and a larger price increase
No quantity change
A larger quantity increase and a smaller price increase
An equal price and quantity change by definition
elite.feedback: More elastic supply absorbs demand shifts through quantity rather than price.

elite.q: Two firms face the same percentage cost increase. Firm A has highly elastic demand; Firm B has inelastic demand. Which firm can pass more of the cost increase on to buyers through a higher price, other things equal?
options: Firm A
Both exactly equally
Neither because cost does not affect price
Firm B
elite.feedback: Customers of Firm B reduce purchases less when price rises.

elite.q: A retailer observes positive cross-price elasticity between its store brand and a national brand. The national brand cuts price. What should the retailer expect for store-brand demand?
options: A decrease
An increase
No change because the goods are substitutes
A shift in store-brand supply
elite.feedback: For substitutes, a fall in one price reduces demand for the other.

elite.q: A restaurant observes negative cross-price elasticity between entrées and desserts. It sharply raises entrée prices. What is the predicted effect on dessert demand?
options: Dessert demand rises
Dessert demand falls
Dessert demand is unchanged because desserts have their own price
Dessert supply shifts right
elite.feedback: Complements are consumed together, so fewer entrées reduce dessert demand.

elite.q: A firm forecasts income growth of 4 percent and estimates income elasticity for its product at 1.5. Holding other factors constant, demand is predicted to:
options: Increase about 2.7 percent
Decrease about 6 percent
Increase about 6 percent
Increase exactly 1.5 percent
elite.feedback: Multiply the income change by the elasticity: 4% × 1.5 = 6%.

elite.q: During a recession, income falls 3 percent. A product has income elasticity −0.8. Demand is predicted to:
options: Decrease about 2.4 percent
Increase about 0.27 percent
Remain unchanged because the coefficient is below one
Increase about 2.4 percent
elite.feedback: A negative coefficient times negative income growth produces a positive demand change.

elite.q: The price of Product Y rises 10 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is −0.5. Demand for X is predicted to:
options: Fall about 5 percent
Rise about 5 percent
Fall about 20 percent
Remain unchanged because the value is negative
elite.feedback: A negative coefficient indicates complements: 10% × −0.5 = −5%.

elite.q: The price of Product Y falls 8 percent. Cross-price elasticity of demand for Product X is 1.25. Demand for X is predicted to:
options: Rise about 10 percent
Fall about 10 percent
Fall about 6.4 percent
Remain unchanged because both are substitutes
elite.feedback: For substitutes, a price decline in Y lowers demand for X: 1.25 × −8% = −10%.

elite.q: A country places a tariff on imports. Import demand is highly elastic. Compared with inelastic import demand, the tariff is likely to produce:
options: A smaller decline in imports and more consumer burden
No change in import quantity
A larger decline in import quantity and less stable tariff revenue
The same effect because tariff rates alone determine quantity
elite.feedback: Elastic import demand responds strongly to the tariff-inclusive price.

elite.q: A union raises the negotiated wage in a labor market where labor demand is highly elastic. Compared with inelastic labor demand, employment is likely to:
options: Fall less sharply
Remain fixed
Rise because wages are higher
Fall more sharply
elite.feedback: Employers substitute away from labor more when labor demand is elastic.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Use the price, quantity, and total-revenue change from C to B. Which elasticity conclusion follows?
options: Demand is inelastic over C–B
Demand is perfectly inelastic over C–B
Demand is elastic over C–B
Demand must have elasticity of zero
elite.feedback: A price decrease that raises total revenue signals elastic demand.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Moving from B to A, use the change in total revenue to classify demand over that segment.
options: Demand is elastic over B–A
Demand is perfectly elastic over B–A
Demand has constant unit elasticity over B–A
Demand is inelastic over B–A
elite.feedback: A price decrease that lowers total revenue signals inelastic demand.

elite.q: After calculating total revenue at A, B, and C from the displayed graph, what elasticity condition is associated with the revenue-maximizing point?
options: Demand is unit elastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Demand is perfectly inelastic
Demand has elasticity greater than 2
elite.feedback: On a linear demand curve, total revenue is maximized at the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic.

elite.q: Calculate total revenue at the two labeled points on D1. What does the change confirm about elasticity?
options: D1 is inelastic over B–A
D1 is perfectly inelastic over B–A
D1 is elastic over B–A
D1 has zero elasticity over B–A
elite.feedback: A price cut that increases total revenue indicates elastic demand.

elite.q: Apply the total-revenue test to the two marked points on D2. How should this interval be classified?
options: D2 is elastic over D–C
D2 is perfectly elastic over D–C
D2 is unit elastic over D–C
D2 is inelastic over D–C
elite.feedback: A price cut that reduces total revenue indicates inelastic demand.

elite.q: For perfectly elastic demand at a market price of $5, what is the idealized result if one seller tries to charge more than $5?
options: Quantity demanded remains fixed at 50
Quantity demanded rises without limit
Quantity demanded falls to zero
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
elite.feedback: With perfectly elastic demand, buyers will not accept a price above the market price represented by the horizontal curve.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Calculate the midpoint price elasticity of supply for the larger long-run quantity response shown.
elite.feedback: The midpoint quantity change is 40/80 = 50% and the price change is 4/6 ≈ 66.7%, giving PES ≈ 0.75.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. After a persistent price increase, quantity supplied initially adjusts toward A and, with more time to respond, toward B. Which elasticity principle does this illustrate?
options: Supply tends to become more elastic over longer time horizons
Supply must become perfectly inelastic over time
Short-run supply is always more elastic than long-run supply over the shown interval
Time horizon affects demand but never supply
elite.feedback: The larger long-run quantity response illustrates that firms can adjust more fully when given time.
