legendary.q: For premium coffee pods, price changes from $0.8 to $0.92 while quantity demanded changes from 100,000 to 82,000. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
options: Elasticity is about 0.71; demand is inelastic, and total revenue moves oppositely
Elasticity is about 1.42; demand is elastic, and total revenue falls
Elasticity is about 0.71; demand is unit elastic, and revenue is unchanged
Elasticity cannot be estimated without a demand equation
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is approximately 1.42. Revenue changes from $80,000 to $75,440, so total revenue falls.

legendary.q: For sports-streaming packages, price changes from $25 to $30 while quantity demanded changes from 60,000 to 43,000. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
options: Elasticity is about 0.55; demand is inelastic, and total revenue moves oppositely
Elasticity is about 0.91; demand is unit elastic, and revenue is unchanged
Elasticity is about 1.82; demand is elastic, and total revenue falls
Elasticity cannot be estimated without a demand equation
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is approximately 1.82. Revenue changes from $1,500,000 to $1,290,000, so total revenue falls.

legendary.q: For pet-grooming appointments, price changes from $55 to $60 while quantity demanded changes from 4,000 to 3,600. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
options: Elasticity is about 0.83; demand is inelastic, and total revenue moves oppositely
Elasticity is about 0.61; demand is unit elastic, and revenue is unchanged
Elasticity cannot be estimated without a demand equation
Elasticity is about 1.21; demand is elastic, and total revenue falls
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is approximately 1.21. Revenue changes from $220,000 to $216,000, so total revenue falls.

legendary.q: For same-day delivery orders, price changes from $12 to $15 while quantity demanded changes from 30,000 to 21,500. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
options: Elasticity is about 1.49; demand is elastic, and total revenue falls
Elasticity is about 0.67; demand is inelastic, and total revenue moves oppositely
Elasticity is about 0.74; demand is unit elastic, and revenue is unchanged
Elasticity cannot be estimated without a demand equation
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is approximately 1.49. Revenue changes from $360,000 to $322,500, so total revenue falls.

legendary.q: At a price of $80, 200 equipment-rental days are supplied. At $100, supply is 220 days this month and 280 after firms expand their fleets. Use midpoint elasticity. Which conclusion fits a buyer seeking 250 rental days at $100?
options: Supply is about 1.50 this month and 0.43 after expansion; only current capacity meets the requirement.
Supply is about 0.43 this month and 1.50 after expansion; only the expanded fleet meets the requirement.
Supply is about 0.43 in both periods because the price change is the same.
Supply is about 1.50 in both periods because any quantity increase is elastic.
legendary.feedback: The common midpoint price change is 20/90. Quantity changes are 20/210 this month and 80/240 after expansion. PES is about 0.43 and 1.50. At $100, 220 is below the required 250, while 280 exceeds it.

legendary.q: The price of beachfront rentals rises from $250 to $300. In the short run, quantity supplied rises from 1,200 to 1,260. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 3.73; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.13; supply is unit elastic
About 0.27; inelastic supply, so producers respond proportionally less than price
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 0.27; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: The price of data-center processing capacity changes from $80 to $96, and quantity supplied changes from 10,000 to 13,000. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 0.7; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.72; supply is unit elastic
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
About 1.43; elastic supply, so producers respond proportionally more than price
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 1.43; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: Over one week, the price of a crate of fresh strawberries rises from $30 to $36, while quantity supplied rises from 5,000 to 5,450 crates. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 0.47; inelastic supply, so producers respond proportionally less than price
About 2.11; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.24; supply is unit elastic
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 0.47; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: The price of recycled aluminum output changes from $2.0 to $2.4, and quantity supplied changes from 80,000 to 100,000. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 0.82; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 1.22; elastic supply, so producers respond proportionally more than price
About 0.61; supply is unit elastic
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 1.22; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: Over a ten-year period, the price of downtown office space rises from $40 to $48, while quantity supplied rises from 200,000 to 245,000. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 0.9; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.56; supply is unit elastic
About 1.11; elastic supply, so producers respond proportionally more than price
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 1.11; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: The price of commercial pilot training slots changes from $15000 to $16500, and quantity supplied changes from 800 to 880. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 1; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.5; supply is unit elastic
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
About 1; unit elastic supply with equal proportional changes
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 1; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: During a season with fixed rainfall, the price of hydroelectric power rises from $50 to $65, while quantity supplied rises from 9,000 to 9,300. Which midpoint elasticity and interpretation are correct?
options: About 0.13; inelastic supply, so producers respond proportionally less than price
About 7.96; the reciprocal must be used for supply
About 0.06; supply is unit elastic
Elasticity is zero because supply slopes upward
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficient is about 0.13; the magnitude determines the classification.

legendary.q: Holding prices fixed, a 4% income increase raises demand for Product A by 6% and lowers demand for Product B by 2%. If income next falls 2%, use the same local elasticities to forecast the two demands approximately.
options: A rises 3% and B falls 1%; A is normal and B is inferior.
A falls 3% and B rises 1%; A is normal and B is inferior.
A falls 3% and B falls 1%; discard both income-elasticity signs.
A falls 1.33% and B rises 4%; use income change divided by demand change.
legendary.feedback: Income elasticities are 6/4 = 1.5 for A and -2/4 = -0.5 for B. Multiplying each signed coefficient by -2% gives -3% and +1%. The signs must be retained for income elasticity.

legendary.q: Household income changes by 5 percent and demand for discount groceries changes by -2 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
options: Income elasticity is -2.5; the product is classified from the reciprocal
Income elasticity is 0.4; the sign has no economic meaning
Income elasticity is -0.4; the product is an inferior good
The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
legendary.feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: -0.4. The sign and magnitude identify an inferior good.

legendary.q: Household income changes by 6 percent and demand for private college housing changes by 5 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
options: Income elasticity is 1.2; the product is classified from the reciprocal
Income elasticity is 0.83; the sign has no economic meaning
The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
Income elasticity is 0.83; the product is an income-inelastic normal good
legendary.feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: 0.83. The sign and magnitude identify an income-inelastic normal good.

legendary.q: Household income changes by 8 percent and demand for used clothing changes by -4 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
options: Income elasticity is -0.5; the product is an inferior good
Income elasticity is -2; the product is classified from the reciprocal
Income elasticity is 0.5; the sign has no economic meaning
The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
legendary.feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: -0.5. The sign and magnitude identify an inferior good.

legendary.q: Household income changes by 3 percent and demand for premium home renovations changes by 7.5 percent. Which estimate and classification are correct?
options: Income elasticity is 0.4; the product is classified from the reciprocal
Income elasticity is 2.5; the product is an income-elastic normal good
Income elasticity is 2.5; the sign has no economic meaning
The product cannot be classified because price is not provided
legendary.feedback: Divide the demand percentage change by the income percentage change: 2.5. The sign and magnitude identify an income-elastic normal good.

legendary.q: Holding other factors fixed, an 8% increase in camera prices reduces demand for a compatible lens by 6%. A supplier next forecasts a 4% camera-price decrease. Which cross-price estimate and approximate lens-demand forecast are consistent?
options: +0.75; lenses and cameras are substitutes, and lens demand falls about 3%.
-0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand falls about 3%.
-0.75; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 3%.
-1.33; lenses and cameras are complements, and lens demand rises about 5.33%.
legendary.feedback: Cross-price elasticity is -6/8 = -0.75. The negative sign indicates complements. Applying the same local estimate to a -4% camera-price change gives (-0.75)(-4%) = +3% lens demand.

legendary.q: A controlled price test finds that an 8% increase in Service Y’s price raises demand for Service X by 10%. If Y next cuts price 4%, which estimate, relationship, and approximate forecast follow?
options: -1.25, complements; demand for X rises about 5%.
+1.25, substitutes; demand for X rises about 5%.
+0.80, substitutes; demand for X falls about 3.2%.
+1.25, substitutes; demand for X falls about 5%.
legendary.feedback: Cross-price elasticity is 10/8 = +1.25. Its positive sign indicates substitutes. Applying that signed estimate to -4% gives a -5% change in X demand, with other factors fixed.

legendary.q: The price of tablet cases changes by 15 percent, and demand for tablets changes by -18 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
options: Cross-price elasticity is -1.2; the goods are complements
Cross-price elasticity is -0.83; the reciprocal defines the relationship
Cross-price elasticity is 1.2; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given
legendary.feedback: The coefficient is -18% ÷ 15% = -1.2. Its sign identifies complements.

legendary.q: Two rival brands have cross-price elasticity +0.8 for A’s demand with respect to B’s price. Brand A expects B to cut price 5%, while income and A’s own price remain fixed. A proposes stocking 4% more units because the coefficient is positive. Evaluate the plan.
options: The sign identifies substitutes and predicts a 4% demand increase, so the stock increase matches the forecast.
The sign identifies substitutes, but the forecast is a 4% demand decrease, so the proposed stock increase reverses the response.
The sign identifies complements and predicts a 4% demand decrease, so the stock increase reverses the response.
The sign identifies substitutes but predicts a 6.25% demand decrease, so division gives the correct forecast.
legendary.feedback: A positive cross-price coefficient means X demand moves in the same direction as the other product’s price. Here 0.8 × (-5%) = -4%. A cheaper substitute reduces demand for A; positive elasticity does not mean demand always increases.

legendary.q: The price of coffee creamer changes by 20 percent, and demand for coffee changes by -7 percent. Which cross-price result is correct?
options: Cross-price elasticity is -2.86; the reciprocal defines the relationship
Cross-price elasticity is 0.35; the goods are substitutes regardless of sign
Cross-price elasticity is -0.35; the goods are complements
The goods are unrelated because neither quantity supplied nor income is given
legendary.feedback: The coefficient is -7% ÷ 20% = -0.35. Its sign identifies complements.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 6 percent price increase with demand elasticity 1.8. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Quantity demanded falls about 3.3 percent and revenue rises
Quantity demanded rises about 10.8 percent
Revenue is unchanged because elasticity is positive
Quantity demanded falls about 10.8 percent and revenue likely falls
legendary.feedback: Multiply 6% by 1.8. Elastic demand makes the percentage quantity loss larger than the price gain.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 5 percent price cut with demand elasticity 0.4. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Quantity demanded rises about 2 percent and revenue likely falls
Quantity demanded rises about 12.5 percent and revenue rises
Quantity demanded falls about 2 percent
Revenue is unchanged because demand is inelastic
legendary.feedback: Quantity changes about 0.4 × 5% = 2%; the price reduction dominates revenue.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 7 percent income increase with income elasticity 1.3. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Demand rises about 5.4 percent
Demand rises about 9.1 percent
Demand falls about 9.1 percent
Demand rises exactly 1.3 percent
legendary.feedback: Multiply 7% by 1.3.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 12 percent increase in a substitute’s price with cross-price elasticity 0.75. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Demand falls about 9 percent
Demand rises about 16 percent
Demand rises about 9 percent
Demand is unchanged because 0.75 is below one
legendary.feedback: Positive cross elasticity means demand moves with the substitute price: 12% × 0.75 = 9%.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 10 percent increase in a complement’s price with cross-price elasticity −0.6. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Demand rises about 6 percent
Demand falls about 16.7 percent
Demand is unchanged because the coefficient is negative
Demand falls about 6 percent

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 9 percent output-price increase with supply elasticity 1.5. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Quantity supplied rises about 13.5 percent
Quantity supplied rises about 6 percent
Quantity supplied falls about 13.5 percent
Quantity supplied rises exactly 1.5 percent
legendary.feedback: Multiply the price change by supply elasticity: 9% × 1.5 = 13.5%.

legendary.q: A planning model assumes a 20 percent wage increase with labor-demand elasticity 0.8. Which forecast is most consistent with the elasticity estimate?
options: Employment rises about 16 percent
Employment falls about 16 percent
Employment falls about 25 percent
Employment is unchanged because labor is a factor market
legendary.feedback: The demand response is 0.8 × 20% = 16% in the opposite direction.

legendary.q: A pharmaceutical patent expires and many close substitutes enter. Holding other determinants constant, what happens to the original brand’s demand elasticity and pricing power?
options: Demand becomes less elastic and markup rises
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic because medicine is necessary
Demand becomes more elastic and sustainable markup falls
Elasticity is unchanged because only price affects demand
legendary.feedback: Entry creates switching options, increasing responsiveness and limiting markup.

legendary.q: A city evaluates a fuel tax using a one-month elasticity estimate. Why might this underestimate the tax’s eventual effect on fuel consumption?
options: Short-run demand always has more substitutes
Long-run elasticity must equal zero
Tax incidence eliminates time-horizon effects
Long-run demand allows vehicle, residence, and commuting adjustments
legendary.feedback: Long-run behavioral and capital adjustments usually increase demand elasticity.

legendary.q: A university raises parking prices and observes little first-semester change, but large declines after students revise housing and transit choices. This illustrates:
options: Demand becoming more elastic over time
Supply becoming perfectly inelastic
Income elasticity turning negative
A movement from elastic to inelastic demand
legendary.feedback: The adjustment menu expands over time.

legendary.q: A national market for all beverages is compared with demand for one flavor of one soda brand. Which statement is strongest?
options: The national beverage market is more elastic because it contains more products
The brand-flavor demand is more elastic because the market is defined narrowly
Both have identical elasticity because they use the same currency
The brand flavor is less elastic because it has fewer buyers
legendary.feedback: Narrow definitions expose many close alternatives.

legendary.q: A firm’s demand curve becomes flatter after a rival enters, but the axes are rescaled at the same time. What is required before concluding that demand became more elastic?
options: Only a visual comparison of slopes
Proof that the rival charges a lower nominal price
A unit-free elasticity calculation at comparable price-quantity points
A calculation of income elasticity
legendary.feedback: Graph scaling can change apparent slope, so percentage responsiveness must be compared.

legendary.q: Two products have identical slopes on graphs measured in different quantity units. Which conclusion is valid?
options: They have identical elasticity everywhere
The product with larger units is more elastic
Both must be unit elastic
No elasticity ranking follows without price and quantity information
legendary.feedback: Slope depends on units; elasticity also uses the point’s P/Q ratio.

legendary.q: Moving down a linear demand curve past the midpoint, what happens to elasticity, marginal revenue, and total revenue?
options: Elasticity falls below one, marginal revenue becomes negative, and total revenue declines as quantity expands
Elasticity rises above one, marginal revenue stays positive, and revenue rises
Elasticity remains one and marginal revenue remains zero
Demand becomes perfectly elastic and revenue becomes infinite
legendary.feedback: Below the midpoint, demand is inelastic and additional sales reduce total revenue.

legendary.q: At the exact unit-elastic point on a smooth demand curve, a very small price change has what first-order effect on total revenue?
options: A guaranteed large increase
Approximately no effect
A guaranteed large decrease
It makes total revenue equal total cost
legendary.feedback: At unit elasticity, opposing price and quantity percentage changes offset.

legendary.q: Why does maximum total revenue not necessarily identify the profit-maximizing output?
options: Revenue and profit are always identical
Elasticity cannot be used by firms
Profit also depends on production costs and marginal cost
The revenue maximum occurs only under perfect competition
legendary.feedback: Profit maximization compares marginal revenue with marginal cost.

legendary.q: A museum has near-zero marginal cost for another visitor before capacity. Why might it still avoid the unit-elastic revenue maximum?
options: Unit elasticity always minimizes revenue
Marginal cost is the only determinant of demand
Elasticity is irrelevant when marginal cost is low
Capacity effects, congestion, mission goals, and segment pricing can change the objective
legendary.feedback: Real pricing may balance revenue with capacity and institutional goals.

legendary.q: A firm charges students less than business travelers for the same flexible software service. The pricing pattern is most sustainable when:
options: The groups can be separated and business demand is less elastic
Students have less elastic demand and resale is costless
Both groups have identical elasticity
Marginal cost is higher for every student user
legendary.feedback: Price discrimination requires separable groups and different elasticities with limited arbitrage.

legendary.q: An airline’s leisure customers become easier to identify, but ticket resale also becomes easy. What happens to elasticity-based price discrimination?
options: Price discrimination becomes stronger automatically
Arbitrage undermines the ability to maintain different prices
Elasticity differences disappear by definition
The airline can ignore resale because seats are services
legendary.feedback: Resale allows low-price buyers to defeat segmentation.

legendary.q: A tax is imposed where demand is less elastic than supply. The statute is rewritten so buyers, rather than sellers, remit it. What happens to economic incidence?
options: The burden shifts entirely to sellers
The burden becomes equal
The burden remains mostly on buyers
The tax disappears from market prices
legendary.feedback: Economic incidence depends on relative elasticity, not remittance rules.

legendary.q: A labor tax is imposed where workers’ labor supply is much less elastic than firms’ labor demand. Who bears most of the burden?
options: Firms through higher labor cost only
The government
Whichever party receives the tax form
Workers through lower after-tax compensation
legendary.feedback: The less elastic side—workers in this case—has fewer avoidance options.

legendary.q: A subsidy is offered to buyers in a market with perfectly inelastic supply. Who captures the subsidy?
options: Sellers through a higher market price
Buyers through a permanently lower net price
The benefit splits equally
No one because quantity cannot rise
legendary.feedback: With fixed supply, competition among buyers bids the subsidy into seller receipts.

legendary.q: A commodity tax raises substantial revenue but creates little deadweight loss. Which combination best explains this?
options: Demand and supply are highly elastic
Demand and supply are relatively inelastic
The tax is collected from producers
The commodity has a positive income elasticity
legendary.feedback: Small quantity responses preserve the tax base and limit lost trades.

legendary.q: A government wants the same revenue from two possible tax bases. Why might it prefer the less elastic base on efficiency grounds?
options: The less elastic base guarantees equal burden sharing
Elasticity determines legal incidence only
The required wedge causes a smaller reduction in traded quantity
The more elastic base has no substitutes
legendary.feedback: A less responsive base distorts fewer trades for a given revenue target.

legendary.q: A congestion charge initially raises revenue but barely reduces traffic. Which change would make it more effective at reducing trips without changing the nominal charge?
options: Making commuting more necessary
Shortening the adjustment period
Reducing information about alternatives
Expansion of reliable transit substitutes
legendary.feedback: Better substitutes raise trip-demand elasticity.

legendary.q: A sugar tax causes consumers to switch to untaxed substitutes. What does this reveal about the elasticity of demand for the taxed product and the design of the tax?
options: Demand is elastic; a broader tax base can limit substitution
Demand is perfectly inelastic, so the tax failed
Supply elasticity alone caused substitution
The statutory payer should be changed
legendary.feedback: Close substitutes generate a strong demand response and can erode a narrow tax base.

legendary.q: A minimum wage has a larger employment effect in one industry than another. Which explanation is most directly elasticity-based?
options: Workers are legally required to pay the wage
Labor demand is more elastic in the industry with the larger employment response
The industry has higher nominal revenue
Labor supply slopes upward in both industries
legendary.feedback: More elastic labor demand produces a larger quantity-of-labor response to wage changes.

legendary.q: Why is labor demand often more elastic when machinery can easily substitute for labor?
options: Machinery makes labor supply more elastic
Wages become a smaller unit of measurement
Firms can change input mix more strongly after a wage increase
The output demand curve becomes vertical
legendary.feedback: Input substitutability raises the responsiveness of labor demanded.

legendary.q: Demand for a firm’s output becomes more elastic. What is the likely effect on the firm’s derived demand for an input used in production?
options: Input demand becomes perfectly inelastic
Input demand becomes unrelated to output price
Input supply becomes less elastic automatically
Input demand becomes more elastic
legendary.feedback: When customers readily reduce output purchases, firms more strongly reduce input use after cost increases.

legendary.q: A country’s export demand is highly elastic. Its currency appreciates, raising foreign-currency export prices. What is the likely quantity effect?
options: A relatively large decline in exports
A small decline because export demand is elastic
No change because exchange rates affect only supply
An increase in exports
legendary.feedback: Elastic foreign demand responds strongly to the higher effective price.

legendary.q: Import supply to a small country is nearly perfectly elastic at the world price. A tariff is introduced. Which side is likely to bear most of the tariff?
options: Foreign suppliers
Domestic import buyers
The burden must be equal
Domestic exporters
legendary.feedback: The highly elastic foreign supply side can redirect goods, leaving domestic buyers with the price increase.

legendary.q: A tariff reduces imports much more than forecast. Which prior assumption was probably too low?
options: The income elasticity of domestic supply
The slope of the world price line in dollars
The price elasticity of import demand
The statutory tariff rate
legendary.feedback: A larger-than-expected quantity response indicates more elastic import demand.

legendary.q: A coffee shortage raises coffee prices, and demand for tea rises sharply. What does this indicate about the relationship between coffee and tea and the sign of their cross-price elasticity?
options: Coffee and tea are complements
Tea is an inferior good
Coffee supply must be perfectly elastic
Tea substitutes for coffee, so cross-price elasticity is positive
legendary.feedback: Switching to tea reveals substitution and a positive cross-price relationship.

legendary.q: The price of smartphones falls, and demand for mobile data plans rises. Which coefficient captures this relationship?
options: A negative cross-price elasticity between phones and data plans
A positive income elasticity for phones
Price elasticity of phone supply
A positive cross-price elasticity because both demands rose
legendary.feedback: A lower phone price raises data-plan demand, so the percentage changes have opposite signs.

legendary.q: An inferior good has income elasticity −0.2. How should the magnitude be interpreted?
options: The good is a strong luxury because the magnitude is below one
Demand responds weakly to income changes, but in the opposite direction
Demand is perfectly income inelastic
The good must be a complement
legendary.feedback: The negative sign indicates inferior; the small magnitude indicates weak responsiveness.

legendary.q: A normal good has income elasticity 0.9. A boom raises income. What is most likely?
options: Demand falls because the coefficient is below one
Demand rises more than proportionally
Demand rises, but less than proportionally
Demand is unaffected
legendary.feedback: Positive but below one means an income-inelastic normal good.

legendary.q: A firm estimates a cross-price elasticity of nearly zero between two products. What is the safest conclusion?
options: They are definitively unrelated in every market and period
They are complements because zero is not positive
They are both necessities
Their demands show little observed relationship in the sampled range
legendary.feedback: Near zero indicates weak measured interaction, not an eternal structural claim.

legendary.q: A demand estimate is elastic at the current price but the firm plans a large price cut. Why is using one constant coefficient risky?
options: Elasticity may change along the demand curve and outside the estimated range
Elasticity always becomes infinite after a price cut
Percentage changes cannot be calculated for price cuts
Only supply elasticity changes with price
legendary.feedback: A local or arc estimate may not extrapolate to a large move.

legendary.q: A regression estimates a price coefficient in levels. Why can that coefficient not automatically be reported as elasticity?
options: Every regression coefficient is already unit-free
Convert it using the current price and quantity scale
Elasticity ignores the price coefficient
Only cross-price coefficients require conversion
legendary.feedback: A level coefficient has units; elasticity is a percentage responsiveness.

legendary.q: A point elasticity is measured on a differentiable demand curve. Which expression combines slope with the current point?
options: The absolute value of (dP/dQ) × (P+Q)
Q divided by P only
The absolute value of (dQ/dP) × (P/Q)
The slope squared
legendary.feedback: Point elasticity scales the derivative by the current price-to-quantity ratio.

legendary.q: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 20, where Q = 60?
options: About 1.50
About 2.00
About 40.00
About 0.67

legendary.q: For demand Q = 100 − 2P, what is elasticity at P = 40, where Q = 20?
legendary.feedback: 2 × 40/20 = 4, so demand is elastic near the price intercept.

legendary.q: For supply Q = 10 + 3P, what is point elasticity at P = 10, where Q = 40?
For supply Q = −20 + 4P, what is point elasticity at P = 10, where Q = 20?
A supply curve passes through the origin and is linear. What is point elasticity along the positive portion?
options: Zero at every point
It rises from zero to infinity
It depends only on the currency unit
One at every point
legendary.feedback: For Q = bP, (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = b(P/bP) = 1.

legendary.q: A linear supply curve intersects the quantity axis at a positive quantity. Along its positive-price region, supply elasticity tends to be:
options: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly one at every point
Negative
legendary.feedback: With Q = a + bP and a > 0, bP/Q < 1.

legendary.q: A linear supply curve has a negative quantity intercept and crosses the price axis above zero. Along its positive-quantity region, supply elasticity tends to be:
options: Less than one
Greater than one
Exactly zero
Negative because the intercept is negative
legendary.feedback: With Q = −a + bP, bP/Q exceeds one where Q is positive.

legendary.q: A farm product has inelastic demand. A bumper crop shifts supply right. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
options: It rises because output always raises revenue
It is unchanged because supply shifted
It falls because the price decline dominates the quantity increase
It becomes equal to consumer surplus
legendary.feedback: With inelastic demand, lower price reduces revenue even as quantity rises.

legendary.q: A farm product has elastic demand. A weather shock shifts supply left. What likely happens to farmers’ total revenue?
options: It rises because price rises
It is unchanged because demand did not shift
It equals tax revenue
It falls because the quantity loss dominates the price increase
legendary.feedback: With elastic demand, the percentage quantity reduction exceeds the price increase.

legendary.q: A platform adds many alternative sellers, reducing buyers’ switching costs. What happens to seller-level demand?
options: It becomes more elastic
It becomes more inelastic
It becomes perfectly inelastic
It changes only income elasticity
legendary.feedback: Lower switching costs and more alternatives raise responsiveness to seller price.

legendary.q: A dominant firm bundles a product with a service that has few substitutes. From an elasticity perspective, how is bundling likely to affect demand for the bundle?
options: Make demand perfectly elastic
Reduce effective substitution and make bundle demand less elastic
Increase cross-price elasticity with rivals
Eliminate the need to consider price
legendary.feedback: Bundling can differentiate the offer and reduce easy comparison.

legendary.q: A loyalty program causes customers to forfeit points if they switch sellers. What is the likely short-run effect on demand elasticity?
options: It raises supply elasticity
It makes income elasticity negative
It lowers demand elasticity by raising switching costs
It creates perfect competition
legendary.feedback: Switching penalties reduce immediate substitution.

legendary.q: A policy analyst uses demand elasticity to predict a quota’s price effect. What additional elasticity is essential?
options: Income elasticity only
Cross-price elasticity only
No other elasticity is relevant
Supply elasticity
legendary.feedback: The equilibrium price response depends on responsiveness on both sides.

legendary.q: A binding production quota reduces market quantity. In which demand case is the price increase likely largest?
options: More inelastic demand
More elastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
Demand with many substitutes
legendary.feedback: When buyers reduce quantity little, price must rise more to clear the restricted supply.

legendary.q: A supply disruption occurs. Which market has the smallest price increase, other things equal?
options: One with inelastic demand and fixed supply
One with elastic demand and elastic supply response from inventories
One with perfectly inelastic demand
One with no substitutes and no stocks
legendary.feedback: Responsive buyers and inventory releases absorb the shock through quantity adjustments.

legendary.q: A firm faces constant-elasticity demand with elasticity 2. Under the inverse-elasticity markup rule, how should its markup compare with the markup when elasticity is 4?
options: A smaller markup because demand is less elastic
The same markup because both are elastic
A larger markup because demand is less elastic
Zero markup because elasticity exceeds one
legendary.feedback: Lower demand elasticity permits a larger price-cost margin.

legendary.q: Why must the absolute demand elasticity exceed one for a standard positive-markup monopolist with positive marginal cost?
options: Because demand would be upward sloping
Because total revenue would be zero
Because supply would become perfectly elastic
Otherwise marginal revenue would be nonpositive at the chosen output
legendary.feedback: Profit maximization with positive marginal cost requires positive marginal revenue, which occurs on the elastic region.

legendary.q: Compare the C→B and B→A intervals on the graph. Why can their elasticity classifications differ?
options: The demand curve has different slopes in the two intervals over the shown interval
The percentage-change bases differ across the two intervals
Elasticity uses only the absolute quantity change
Elasticity is determined only by the direction of price
legendary.feedback: Elasticity depends on percentage changes, so identical absolute changes can produce different elasticities when the average price and quantity bases differ.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A seller at A can choose the posted price at A, B, or C and can serve all buyers. It wants higher revenue while retaining at least 50 unit sales. Which price is best, and what explains the result?
options: The price at C; its highest posted price also gives the highest revenue and meets the minimum.
The price at A; its largest quantity necessarily gives the highest revenue.
The price at B; revenue rises by 120 while sales remain above the minimum.
The price at B; revenue stays unchanged but sales rise above their level at A.
legendary.feedback: A earns 4 × 90 = 360, B earns 8 × 60 = 480, and C earns 12 × 30 = 360. B raises revenue by 120 and sells 60 units. C also fails the 50-unit minimum. The A-to-B interval is inelastic, so the price increase raises revenue.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A seller at C can instead post the price at A or B, but capacity is limited to 70 units and sales equal the smaller of demand and capacity. Which change earns more revenue, and why is demand elasticity alone insufficient?
options: Move to A: revenue is 360; all 90 demanded units can be sold.
Move to A: revenue is 480; a larger price cut guarantees a larger revenue increase.
Stay at C: revenue is 480; capacity makes the B price infeasible.
Move to B: revenue is 480; at A capacity limits revenue to 280.
legendary.feedback: At B, 60 units are demanded and can be sold, earning 8 × 60 = 480. At A, demand is 90 but only 70 can be sold, earning 4 × 70 = 280. C earns 360. Elasticity describes demand, while a binding sales constraint changes realized revenue.

legendary.q: Use the labeled intervals to calculate midpoint elasticity on D1 and D2. Which statement follows?
options: Only D1 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Only D2 is above the unit-elastic threshold
Both are exactly unit elastic
Neither curve can be classified
legendary.feedback: Elasticity above one is elastic; 1.43 exceeds one while 0.89 does not.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. Two otherwise comparable products face D1 and D2 over the marked $10-to-$6 interval. Which pairing of substitute availability and revenue response is consistent with midpoint elasticity?
options: D2 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut raises D1 revenue but lowers D2 revenue.
D1 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut raises D1 revenue but lowers D2 revenue.
D1 plausibly has more close substitutes; the price cut lowers D1 revenue but raises D2 revenue.
Both have the same responsiveness; equal price changes make both revenues unchanged.
legendary.feedback: The midpoint coefficients are about 1.43 for D1 and 0.89 for D2. More substitutes is a plausible explanation for D1’s greater responsiveness, not proof from slope alone. Revenue changes from 450 to 570 on D1 and from 350 to 330 on D2.

legendary.q: How do the absolute elasticity magnitudes of D1 and D2 compare?
options: Both equal one
D1 equals zero while D2 approaches infinity
Both equal zero
D1 approaches infinity while D2 equals zero
legendary.feedback: Perfectly elastic demand is the infinite-elasticity limiting case; perfectly inelastic demand has elasticity zero.

legendary.q: Refer to the graph. A buyer needs 90 units when price has risen from the common starting point to $8. Using midpoint supply elasticities, which comparison and procurement conclusion are supported?
options: Short run about 0.75, long run 0.23; 90 units can be supplied only in the short run.
Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; 90 units can be supplied only after the longer adjustment.
Short run about 0.23, long run 0.75; neither horizon can supply 90 units at $8.
Short run about 0.23, long run 1.33; longer-run supply is elastic because it is flatter.
legendary.feedback: Starting quantity is 60 at $4. At $8, short-run quantity is 70 and long-run quantity is 100. Midpoint PES is (10/65)/(4/6) ≈ 0.23 and (40/80)/(4/6) = 0.75. Both are inelastic over this interval, but only the long run reaches the 90-unit requirement.
