consumer-and-producer-surplus.title: Consumer and Producer Surplus
consumer-and-producer-surplus.description: Explain and calculate consumer surplus, producer surplus, total surplus, gains from exchange, efficient quantity, allocation, and efficiency-equity distinctions.

objectiveLabels.CPS.1: Explain willingness to pay, willingness to accept, consumer surplus, and producer surplus.
objectiveLabels.CPS.2: Calculate consumer, producer, and total surplus from schedules, tables, and graphs.
objectiveLabels.CPS.3: Identify marginal buyers, marginal sellers, mutually beneficial exchanges, and the efficient quantity.
objectiveLabels.CPS.4: Analyze how price and quantity changes redistribute or reduce surplus.
objectiveLabels.CPS.5: Evaluate market efficiency, equity, and the limits of surplus analysis.
objectiveLabels.CPS.6: Apply surplus analysis to bounded adjacent-market policies without requiring later-course machinery.

easy.q: Which statement defines willingness to pay?
options: The maximum amount a buyer would voluntarily pay
The amount every buyer actually pays
The minimum amount a seller will accept
The seller’s total revenue
easy.feedback: Willingness to pay is the buyer’s maximum acceptable payment.

easy.q: Which statement defines willingness to accept?
options: The price every seller actually receives
The minimum amount a seller would voluntarily accept
The maximum amount a buyer will pay
The seller’s total fixed cost
easy.feedback: Willingness to accept is the seller’s minimum acceptable payment.

easy.q: Consumer surplus is calculated as:
options: Price paid minus willingness to pay
Price paid plus willingness to pay
Willingness to pay minus the price paid
Seller revenue minus buyer value
easy.feedback: Consumer surplus is buyer value minus price.

easy.q: Producer surplus is calculated as:
options: Willingness to accept minus price received
Price received plus willingness to accept
Buyer value minus seller revenue
Price received minus willingness to accept
easy.feedback: Producer surplus is price minus minimum acceptable amount.

easy.q: Total surplus in a market equals:
options: Consumer surplus plus producer surplus
Consumer surplus minus producer surplus
Market revenue plus total cost
The price times every possible unit
easy.feedback: Total surplus adds buyer and seller gains.

easy.q: Ava is willing to pay at most $18 for a concert ticket. The market price is $12. What is the outcome?
options: $12 of consumer surplus
$6 of consumer surplus
$18 of consumer surplus
$30 of consumer surplus
easy.feedback: Ava values the concert ticket at $18 and pays $12, so consumer surplus is $6.

easy.q: Ben is willing to pay at most $25 for a used textbook. The market price is $17. What is the outcome?
options: $17 of consumer surplus
$25 of consumer surplus
$8 of consumer surplus
$42 of consumer surplus
easy.feedback: Ben values the used textbook at $25 and pays $17, so consumer surplus is $8.

easy.q: Cam is willing to pay at most $14 for a farmers-market basket. The market price is $14. What is the outcome?
options: $14 of consumer surplus
$28 of consumer surplus
$7 of consumer surplus
$0 of consumer surplus
easy.feedback: Cam values the farmers-market basket at $14 and pays $14, so consumer surplus is $0.

easy.q: Dina is willing to pay at most $11 for a bike tune-up. The market price is $15. What is the outcome?
options: No purchase; the price exceeds willingness to pay
A purchase with $4 of consumer surplus
A purchase with $15 of consumer surplus
A purchase with $11 of consumer surplus
easy.feedback: The price exceeds Dina’s willingness to pay, so the purchase does not occur.

easy.q: Alba will provide one museum pass only for at least $7. The market price is $12. What is the outcome?
options: $12 of producer surplus
$5 of producer surplus
$7 of producer surplus
$19 of producer surplus
easy.feedback: Alba receives $12 and requires at least $7, so producer surplus is $5.

easy.q: Brock will provide one meal-kit box only for at least $15. The market price is $21. What is the outcome?
options: $21 of producer surplus
$15 of producer surplus
$6 of producer surplus
$36 of producer surplus
easy.feedback: Brock receives $21 and requires at least $15, so producer surplus is $6.

easy.q: Cora will provide one tutoring session only for at least $10. The market price is $10. What is the outcome?
options: $10 of producer surplus
$20 of producer surplus
$5 of producer surplus
$0 of producer surplus
easy.feedback: Cora receives $10 and requires at least $10, so producer surplus is $0.

easy.q: Dev will provide one theater seat only for at least $16. The market price is $13. What is the outcome?
options: No sale; the price is below willingness to accept
A sale with $3 of producer surplus
A sale with $13 of producer surplus
A sale with $16 of producer surplus
easy.feedback: The market price is below Dev’s minimum acceptable amount, so the sale does not occur.

easy.q: A buyer values a museum pass at $30 and pays $22. Which number is the buyer’s willingness to pay?
easy.feedback: The buyer’s maximum value is $30.

easy.q: A seller would provide a meal-kit box for no less than $9 and receives $14. Which number is willingness to accept?
easy.feedback: The minimum acceptable amount is $9.

easy.q: At the market price, the marginal buyer is the buyer who:
options: Has the highest willingness to pay
Receives the largest consumer surplus
Would buy every unit
Is just willing to purchase the last unit traded
easy.feedback: The marginal buyer is at the trading cutoff.

easy.q: At the market price, the marginal seller is the seller who:
options: Is just willing to provide the last unit traded
Has the lowest cost
Receives the largest producer surplus
Would supply every unit
easy.feedback: The marginal seller is at the trading cutoff.

easy.q: A voluntary exchange creates gains when:
options: Seller cost exceeds buyer value
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
Price exceeds both value and cost
Buyer and seller surplus are equal
easy.feedback: Value must cover cost.

easy.q: Why does a buyer with willingness to pay below price normally not purchase?
options: The buyer would receive producer surplus
The seller would have zero revenue
The exchange would give the buyer negative consumer surplus
The market would lower price automatically
easy.feedback: Paying above value creates negative buyer surplus.

easy.q: Why does a seller with willingness to accept above price normally not sell?
options: The buyer would receive zero surplus
The seller would earn the largest surplus
The market would raise price automatically
The exchange would give the seller negative producer surplus
easy.feedback: Receiving below cost creates negative seller surplus.

easy.q: On a standard graph, consumer surplus lies:
options: Below demand and above price through the quantity traded
Above demand and above price
Below supply and below price
Beyond the quantity traded
easy.feedback: Consumer surplus is the value-price gap on traded units.

easy.q: On a standard graph, producer surplus lies:
options: Below supply and below price
Above supply and below price through the quantity traded
Above demand and above price
Beyond the quantity traded
easy.feedback: Producer surplus is the price-cost gap on traded units.

easy.q: In the standard competitive model, the efficient quantity is reached where:
options: Every buyer receives zero surplus
Every seller receives equal surplus
Marginal willingness to pay equals marginal willingness to accept
The price is judged fair
easy.feedback: Efficiency stops where marginal value equals marginal cost.

easy.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes efficiency from equity?
options: Both require equal surplus
Efficiency concerns only price
Equity always maximizes total surplus
Efficiency concerns total surplus; equity concerns distribution
easy.feedback: Efficiency and equity answer different questions.

easy.q: A market can maximize total surplus and still be criticized because:
options: The gains may be distributed very unevenly
Every efficient market has zero consumer surplus
Efficiency requires identical incomes
Producer surplus must exceed consumer surplus
easy.feedback: Efficiency does not settle fairness.

easy.q: Why is demand used to measure consumer surplus?
options: It records seller revenue
It represents marginal willingness to pay for successive units
It measures fixed costs
It counts firms
easy.feedback: Demand height represents marginal buyer value.

easy.q: Why is supply used to measure producer surplus?
options: It records buyer income
It shows consumer surplus directly
It represents marginal willingness to accept or marginal cost
It measures maximum buyer value
easy.feedback: Supply height represents marginal seller cost.

easy.q: If willingness to pay exactly equals price, the buyer receives:
options: Maximum consumer surplus
Negative producer surplus
Surplus equal to price
Zero consumer surplus
easy.feedback: The difference is zero.

easy.q: If willingness to accept exactly equals price, the seller receives:
options: Zero producer surplus
Maximum producer surplus
Negative consumer surplus
Surplus equal to revenue
easy.feedback: The difference is zero.

easy.q: When two identical units are available, which buyer allocation maximizes measured surplus?
options: Give them to the two buyers with the lowest willingness to pay
Give them to the two buyers with the highest willingness to pay
Assign them randomly regardless of value
Give both to the marginal seller
easy.feedback: Higher buyer values create greater total surplus when costs are unchanged.

easy.q: Total surplus measures the combined gains received by:
options: Sellers only
Government only
Buyers and sellers
Buyers only
easy.feedback: Total surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus.

easy.q: A market creates $40 of gains for buyers and $35 of gains for sellers. Which welfare measure combines both sets of gains?
options: Total revenue
Total surplus
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
easy.feedback: Total surplus combines the gains received by buyers and sellers.

easy.q: A trade creates $12 of consumer surplus and $9 of producer surplus. The gain from that trade is:
easy.feedback: The total gain from exchange is the sum of the buyer’s and seller’s surplus.

easy.q: A voluntary trade is mutually beneficial when:
options: The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the buyer’s willingness to pay
The market price is zero
Consumer surplus must equal producer surplus
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least as high as the seller’s willingness to accept
easy.feedback: A trade can create gains when the buyer values the unit at least as much as the seller’s opportunity cost.

easy.q: If a transaction creates no consumer surplus but $6 of producer surplus, total surplus from that transaction is:
options: Cannot be positive unless both sides receive surplus
easy.feedback: Total surplus adds the gains of both sides; one side may receive all of the measured surplus.

easy.q: Which statement about total surplus is correct?
options: It ignores all gains from voluntary exchange
It can rise even if one side receives a smaller share of the gains
It rises only when consumer and producer surplus rise by identical amounts
It is the same thing as total revenue
easy.feedback: Efficiency concerns the size of total gains, not whether those gains are split evenly.

easy.q: If a mutually beneficial trade is prevented, the unrealized gain is best described as:
options: Lost total surplus
A transfer from buyer to seller
Higher total revenue
Producer surplus that still exists
easy.feedback: Preventing a beneficial trade destroys the buyer-seller gain that would otherwise be created.

easy.q: Consumer surplus falls by $8 while producer surplus rises by $8 and no trades are lost. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $16
Rises by $16
Must become zero
Does not change
easy.feedback: An equal transfer between buyers and sellers changes distribution but not the combined surplus.

easy.q: In an efficient allocation, a unit should be produced when:
options: The market price is below zero
Consumer and producer surplus must be equal
The buyer’s willingness to pay is at least the seller’s willingness to accept
The seller’s willingness to accept exceeds every buyer’s willingness to pay
easy.feedback: Production creates a nonnegative gain when value to the buyer covers the seller’s opportunity cost.

easy.q: Efficiency requires goods to go to buyers who:
options: Always pay the highest possible price
Value them most highly as measured by willingness to pay
Have the lowest willingness to pay
Arrive first regardless of value
easy.feedback: Allocating units to higher-value buyers maximizes measured gains from consumption.

easy.q: Efficiency requires production by sellers who:
options: Can supply at the lowest opportunity cost
Have the highest willingness to accept
Charge the highest price
Receive the largest fixed subsidy
easy.feedback: Using lower-cost sellers preserves more surplus from each unit produced.

easy.q: Once the next seller’s willingness to accept exceeds the next buyer’s willingness to pay, producing one more unit would:
options: Increase total surplus
Leave total surplus unchanged by definition
Create consumer surplus with no cost
Reduce total surplus
easy.feedback: The next unit costs more to produce than the buyer values it, so it destroys surplus.

easy.q: The efficient quantity is the quantity that:
options: Maximizes consumer surplus only
Guarantees equal incomes
Maximizes total surplus
Maximizes producer surplus only
easy.feedback: Efficiency in this model is defined by maximizing the combined gains from exchange.

easy.q: If the next unit has willingness to pay of $26 and willingness to accept of $20, producing that unit would:
options: Have no effect on total surplus
Add $6 to total surplus
Reduce total surplus by $6
Transfer $46 from buyer to seller
easy.feedback: The gain from the unit is $26 - $20 = $6.

easy.q: If a policy merely transfers $10 of surplus from buyers to sellers and no trades change, total surplus:
options: Must equal zero
Is unchanged
Falls by $10
Rises by $10
easy.feedback: A pure transfer changes who receives surplus, not the combined amount.

easy.q: If a policy prevents mutually beneficial trades, total surplus generally:
options: Falls
Rises
Is guaranteed to stay constant
Becomes equal to government revenue
easy.feedback: Prevented beneficial exchanges eliminate gains that would otherwise exist.

easy.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, consumer surplus generally:
options: Rises
Must stay constant
Becomes producer surplus one-for-one in every case
Falls
easy.feedback: Buyers pay more for the same units, reducing their value-minus-price gains.

easy.q: When market price rises and the same units continue to trade, producer surplus generally:
options: Must stay constant
Becomes consumer surplus
Rises
Falls
easy.feedback: Sellers receive a higher price relative to their willingness to accept.

easy.q: A policy causes some trades with positive gains to disappear. The value of those lost gains is:
options: Guaranteed government revenue
A loss in total surplus
A pure transfer between buyers and sellers
Additional consumer surplus
easy.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades reduce the combined gains available in the market.

easy.q: A market outcome can maximize total surplus but still raise concerns about:
options: Whether buyers have preferences
Equity or distribution
Whether any exchange occurred
Whether prices exist
easy.feedback: Efficiency and equity are different criteria; maximizing total gains does not determine how those gains are shared.

easy.q: Why can willingness to pay understate the importance of a good to a low-income consumer?
options: Ability to pay can constrain the amount the consumer can bid
Willingness to pay never reflects preferences
Low-income consumers always have zero consumer surplus
Market prices automatically correct income differences
easy.feedback: Observed willingness to pay reflects both preferences and purchasing power.

easy.q: Surplus analysis by itself does not determine whether an outcome is:
options: Efficient in the total-surplus sense
Based on voluntary exchange
Associated with gains from trade
Fair
easy.feedback: Total surplus is an efficiency measure, not a complete theory of fairness.

medium.q: Each buyer wants at most one concert ticket. Willingness to pay is Ava $24, Ben $19, Cam $12. At a price of $15, what is total consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 buyers purchase. Their value-price gaps total $13.

medium.q: Each buyer wants at most one used textbook. Willingness to pay is Dina $30, Eli $23, Fern $17, Gus $9. At a price of $18, what is total consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 buyers purchase. Their value-price gaps total $17.

medium.q: Each buyer wants at most one museum pass. Willingness to pay is Hana $16, Ivan $14, Jules $8. At a price of $10, what is total consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 buyers purchase. Their value-price gaps total $10.

medium.q: Each buyer wants at most one fitness class. Willingness to pay is Kai $27, Lena $21, Mia $15, Noah $11. At a price of $16, what is total consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 buyers purchase. Their value-price gaps total $16.

medium.q: Each seller can provide at most one farmers-market basket. Minimum acceptable amounts are Alba $5, Brock $9, Cora $14. At a price of $11, what is total producer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 sellers participate. Their price-cost gaps total $8.

medium.q: Each seller can provide at most one bike tune-up. Minimum acceptable amounts are Dev $6, Esme $10, Finn $13, Gia $19. At a price of $14, what is total producer surplus?
medium.feedback: 3 sellers participate. Their price-cost gaps total $13.

medium.q: Each seller can provide at most one meal-kit box. Minimum acceptable amounts are Hugo $8, Inez $12, Jae $17. At a price of $13, what is total producer surplus?
medium.feedback: 2 sellers participate. Their price-cost gaps total $6.

medium.q: Each seller can provide at most one garden service. Minimum acceptable amounts are Kira $4, Leo $9, Mara $15, Nico $21. At a price of $16, what is total producer surplus?
medium.feedback: 3 sellers participate. Their price-cost gaps total $20.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is consumer surplus at the competitive equilibrium?
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $32.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is producer surplus at the competitive equilibrium?
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $32.

medium.q: Combine the two surplus regions in the balanced graph. What total surplus results?
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $64.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is consumer surplus at the asymmetric competitive equilibrium?
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $64.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. What is producer surplus at the asymmetric competitive equilibrium?
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $32.

medium.q: Add consumer and producer surplus in the compact equilibrium graph.
medium.feedback: The relevant area equals $50.

medium.q: Four buyers value permits at $28, $22, $16, and $10. At a price of $16, who is marginal?
options: The buyer with willingness to pay of $16
The $28 buyer
The $10 buyer
All four buyers
medium.feedback: The $16 buyer is at the cutoff.

medium.q: Four sellers have costs of $5, $9, $13, and $18. At a price of $13, who is marginal?
options: The $5 seller
The seller with a cost of $13
The $18 seller
All sellers below $18
medium.feedback: The $13 seller is at the cutoff.

medium.q: A buyer values a service at $40 and seller cost is $24. What gain is available?
medium.feedback: Buyer value minus seller cost is $16.

medium.q: A buyer values a service at $18 and seller cost is $23. Which conclusion follows?
options: The exchange creates $5
The exchange creates $41
Any price from $18 to $23 is efficient
The exchange should not occur because it would reduce total surplus by $5
medium.feedback: Cost exceeds value by $5.

medium.q: If price rises while the same units continue to trade, what usually happens?
options: Some consumer surplus is transferred to producers
Total surplus must rise
Producer surplus falls
All consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss
medium.feedback: With unchanged trades, price redistributes surplus.

medium.q: If price falls while the same units continue to trade, what usually happens?
options: Total surplus must fall
Some producer surplus is transferred to consumers
Consumer surplus falls
All producer surplus becomes deadweight loss
medium.feedback: With unchanged trades, price redistributes surplus.

medium.q: Why is output below the efficient quantity inefficient?
options: Every seller has negative surplus
Price must be negative
Some units valued above cost are not traded
Consumer and producer surplus must be equal
medium.feedback: Underproduction misses positive-gain units.

medium.q: Why is output above the efficient quantity inefficient?
options: Every buyer has negative surplus
Price must exceed every value
Producer surplus must be zero
Some units cost more than buyers value them
medium.feedback: Overproduction includes negative-gain units.

medium.q: Which buyer allocation is efficient for three identical units?
options: Give them to the three highest-value buyers
Give them to the three lowest-value buyers
Assign them randomly
Give all to the lowest-income buyer
medium.feedback: Highest buyer values maximize total value.

medium.q: Which seller assignment is efficient for three units?
options: Use the three highest-cost sellers
Use the three lowest-cost sellers
Use every seller once
Use the seller with highest fixed cost
medium.feedback: Lowest costs maximize total surplus.

medium.q: Consumer surplus is $70 and producer surplus is $45. Total surplus is:
medium.feedback: Add $70 and $45.

medium.q: Consumer surplus rises from $80 to $95 while producer surplus falls from $60 to $40. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $15
Falls by $20
Is unchanged
Falls by $5
medium.feedback: Total changes from $140 to $135.

medium.q: Why can willingness to pay be an incomplete measure of social importance?
options: It can reflect ability to pay as well as value
It is identical for every buyer
It measures seller cost
It cannot be expressed in money
medium.feedback: Income can constrain dollar willingness to pay.

medium.q: Why is producer surplus not always accounting profit?
options: Revenue is excluded from producer surplus
Fixed costs may reduce profit even when producer surplus is positive
Producer surplus counts buyer value
Profit ignores costs
medium.feedback: Profit also subtracts fixed costs.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Why is E efficient under the standard assumptions?
options: Every buyer gets equal surplus
Every seller gets equal surplus
The value of the last unit equals its cost
The price is the highest possible
medium.feedback: Demand and supply meet at equal marginal value and cost.

medium.q: Refer to the graph. Which area is buyer expenditure at equilibrium?
options: The triangle above price
The triangle below price
The entire area between demand and supply
The rectangle with height $10 and width 8
medium.feedback: Expenditure is price times quantity.

medium.q: Jordan is willing to pay $42 for a textbook and buys it for $31. What is Jordan’s consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: Consumer surplus is willingness to pay minus the price paid: $42 - $31 = $11.

medium.q: Three buyers value a pass at $30, $24, and $18. The market price is $22 and each buys at most one. What is total consumer surplus?
medium.feedback: The first two buyers purchase and receive surpluses of $8 and $2, totaling $10.

medium.q: A buyer would pay up to $75 for a repair but the market price is $68. If the buyer purchases, the $7 difference represents:
options: Total revenue
Deadweight loss
Consumer surplus
Producer surplus
medium.feedback: The value above the price actually paid is the buyer’s consumer surplus.

medium.q: A seller is willing to provide a service for at least $28 and receives a market price of $36. What is the seller’s producer surplus?
medium.feedback: Producer surplus is price received minus willingness to accept: $36 - $28 = $8.

medium.q: Three sellers have willingness to accept of $9, $14, and $21. The market price is $18 and each can sell one unit. What is total producer surplus?
medium.feedback: The first two sellers trade and earn $9 and $4 of producer surplus, totaling $13.

medium.q: A producer would supply a unit for at least $16 and receives $22. The $6 difference is:
options: Consumer surplus
Economic profit including every fixed cost
Deadweight loss
Producer surplus
medium.feedback: Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.

medium.q: A market change raises consumer surplus by $18 and lowers producer surplus by $10. What happens to total surplus?
options: It is unchanged
It rises by $28
It rises by $8
It falls by $28
medium.feedback: The net change in total surplus is +$18 - $10 = +$8.

medium.q: A buyer values a unit at $70, a seller’s willingness to accept is $52, and they trade at $60. What is total surplus from the trade?
medium.feedback: Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.

medium.q: Two possible trades have WTP/WTA pairs of $50/$32 and $40/$38. If both trades occur, what is total gain from exchange?
medium.feedback: The gains are $18 and $2, totaling $20.

medium.q: A rule transfers $15 of surplus from consumers to producers but also prevents trades worth $6 in total gains. What is the net change in total surplus?
options: An increase of $9
An increase of $15
No change because transfers never matter
A decrease of $6
medium.feedback: The $15 transfer changes distribution only; the prevented trades destroy $6 of total surplus.

medium.q: Four buyers value a unit at $40, $32, $25, and $18. Four sellers have costs of $12, $20, $27, and $35. Pairing highest-value buyers with lowest-cost sellers, how many trades are efficient?
medium.feedback: The first two trades have WTP above cost; the third would have WTP $25 below cost $27.

medium.q: A market currently produces 6 units. The seventh unit has WTP $44 and WTA $39; the eighth has WTP $36 and WTA $41. What is the efficient quantity?
options: 6 units
8 units
The quantity cannot be determined from marginal values
7 units
medium.feedback: The seventh adds $5 of surplus, while the eighth would destroy $5.

medium.q: Two allocation plans produce the same number of units. Plan A gives the units to buyers with WTP $30 and $28; Plan B gives them to buyers with WTP $30 and $20. Production costs are identical. Which plan is more efficient?
options: Both are equally efficient because quantity is the same
Efficiency depends only on seller surplus
Plan A
Plan B
medium.feedback: With identical costs, allocating the second unit to the buyer with WTP $28 creates more total surplus.

medium.q: A policy transfers $22 of surplus from consumers to producers and, separately, prevents trades worth $9 in total gains. Compared with the original market, total surplus changes by:
medium.feedback: The $22 transfer changes distribution only; the separately lost trades reduce total surplus by $9.

medium.q: A price change transfers $30 from consumers to producers and also reduces mutually beneficial trades by $12. What is the efficiency effect?
options: Total surplus rises by $18
Total surplus falls by $42
Total surplus is unchanged
Total surplus falls by $12
medium.feedback: The $30 is a transfer; only the $12 of lost gains reduces total surplus.

medium.q: A rule lowers consumer surplus by $25 and raises producer surplus by $19. If there are no other gains or losses, what happened to total surplus?
options: It rose by $6
It was unchanged
It fell by $6
It rose by $44
medium.feedback: Add the changes: -$25 + $19 = -$6.

medium.q: Two policies generate the same total surplus, but one gives nearly all gains to high-income buyers while the other spreads gains broadly. Surplus analysis alone can conclude that:
options: The second policy is necessarily more efficient because gains are spread broadly
Neither policy can be compared in any way
They are equally efficient by total surplus, but it cannot settle the equity comparison
The first policy is necessarily better because buyers have more income
medium.feedback: Equal total surplus means equal measured efficiency, while distribution requires an additional normative criterion.

medium.q: Suppose a market creates pollution costs not borne by buyers or sellers. Why can ordinary consumer-plus-producer surplus overstate social surplus?
options: It automatically subtracts taxes from surplus
It omits part of the external cost
It counts willingness to pay twice
It treats every seller as identical
medium.feedback: Private surplus measures can miss costs imposed on third parties.

medium.q: A rich buyer outbids a poor buyer for a scarce medicine even though the poor buyer’s health benefit would be larger. What limitation does this illustrate?
options: Willingness to pay depends partly on ability to pay
Total surplus can never be calculated
Producer surplus is always negative in health markets
Efficiency and scarcity are unrelated
medium.feedback: Dollar willingness to pay is constrained by income and may not measure all dimensions of social value.

medium.q: An economist reports that Policy A yields $500 of total surplus and Policy B yields $470. What can be concluded without additional value judgments?
options: Policy A is necessarily fairer
Policy B must have more consumer surplus
Policy A must make every person better off
Policy A has higher measured efficiency under the surplus criterion
medium.feedback: The total-surplus comparison speaks to measured efficiency, not fairness or individual gains.

hard.q: Each participant trades at most one home-repair visit. Buyer values are Ava $42, Ben $33, Cam $25, Dina $14. Seller costs are Alba $8, Brock $17, Cora $29, Dev $38. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 4 trades and $22 of total surplus
2 trades and $75 of total surplus
2 trades and $50 of total surplus
1 trade and $34 of total surplus
hard.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $50 total surplus.

hard.q: Each participant trades at most one festival wristband. Buyer values are Eli $38, Fern $31, Gus $23, Hana $17, Ivan $9. Seller costs are Esme $5, Finn $12, Gia $20, Hugo $28, Inez $36. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 5 trades and $17 of total surplus
3 trades and $92 of total surplus
2 trades and $52 of total surplus
3 trades and $55 of total surplus
hard.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 3 trades create $55 total surplus.

hard.q: Each participant trades at most one meal-kit box. Buyer values are Jules $34, Kai $26, Lena $19, Mia $10. Seller costs are Jae $7, Kira $15, Leo $22, Mara $30. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 2 trades and $38 of total surplus
4 trades and $15 of total surplus
2 trades and $60 of total surplus
1 trade and $27 of total surplus
hard.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 2 trades create $38 total surplus.

hard.q: Each participant trades at most one parking space. Buyer values are Noah $45, Omar $37, Pia $28, Quinn $18, Rae $11. Seller costs are Nico $6, Opal $14, Pax $24, Rina $33, Sol $41. What efficient outcome maximizes total surplus?
options: 5 trades and $21 of total surplus
3 trades and $66 of total surplus
3 trades and $110 of total surplus
2 trades and $62 of total surplus
hard.feedback: Pair highest buyer values with lowest seller costs. The first 3 trades create $66 total surplus.

hard.q: Refer to the balanced-market graph. Which amount and region represent consumer surplus at E?
options: $32, below demand and above the market price, up to the traded quantity
$32, above supply and below the market price, up to the traded quantity
$80, the price-times-quantity rectangle
$64, the entire region between demand and supply up to E
hard.feedback: At E, quantity is 8 and price is $10. Consumer surplus is 0.5 × 8 × ($18 − $10) = $32. The equally sized area above supply is producer surplus; expenditure is $80 and total surplus is $64.

hard.q: Which expression correctly calculates producer surplus in the asymmetric equilibrium graph?
hard.feedback: Producer surplus is the triangle below the $14 equilibrium price and above supply through Q = 8.

hard.q: Refer to the compact-market graph. At E, what is total surplus, and why is it different from buyer expenditure?
options: $50; it measures value above production cost, rather than payments
$70; it equals the price paid for all units
$25; it includes only the area above the price
$100; it is the full intercept-gap rectangle
hard.feedback: The graph gives Q = 5, P = $14, demand intercept $24 and supply intercept $4. CS and PS are each $25, so total surplus is $50. Payments of $70 transfer money between market participants.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Output is limited to 6 units. What is true about units 7 and 8?
options: Their cost exceeds value, so omitting them raises surplus
Their marginal value exceeds marginal cost, so omitting them loses $4 of total surplus
They transfer $4 from producers to consumers
No loss can be measured
hard.feedback: Between Q=6 and Q=8, demand lies above supply; the missing triangle is $4.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Output is pushed to 10 units. What is true about units 9 and 10?
options: Their value exceeds cost, so they add $4
They transfer $4 from consumers to producers
Their marginal cost exceeds value, so producing them destroys $4 of total surplus
More output is always efficient
hard.feedback: Between Q=8 and Q=10, supply lies above demand; the excess-cost triangle is $4.

hard.q: A price change raises producer surplus by $30 and lowers consumer surplus by $30, with no quantity change. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $30
Falls by $30
Falls by $60
Is unchanged
hard.feedback: The equal gain and loss are a transfer.

hard.q: A restriction raises producer surplus by $24 and lowers consumer surplus by $39. The change in total surplus is:
options: A decrease of $15
An increase of $24
A decrease of $39
No change
hard.feedback: Add +$24 and -$39.

hard.q: Buyer values are $50, $36, and $22; seller costs are $12, $28, and $25. Which exchanges are efficient?
options: All three
The first two only
The first only
The second and third only
hard.feedback: The gains are $38, $8, and -$3.

hard.q: A price rise causes one low-value buyer to leave and one high-cost seller to enter. Why can total surplus change?
options: Any price rise raises total surplus
Surplus stops existing
The set of exchanges changes, so the effect is not only a transfer
The outcome becomes equitable
hard.feedback: Participation changes can create or destroy gains.

hard.q: Why does competitive equilibrium maximize total surplus in the basic model?
options: It makes consumer and producer surplus equal
It gives everyone equal income
It chooses the lowest price
It includes every unit with value at least cost and excludes units with cost above value
hard.feedback: The equilibrium cutoff separates positive- and negative-gain units.

hard.q: A scarce unit goes to a buyer valuing it at $18 instead of one valuing it at $31. Cost is unchanged. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $13
Rises by $13
Is unchanged
Falls by $49
hard.feedback: Buyer value falls by $13.

hard.q: A unit is produced by a seller with cost $27 instead of an available seller with cost $16. Buyer value is unchanged. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $11
Falls by $11
Is unchanged
Falls by $43
hard.feedback: Resource cost rises by $11.

hard.q: Why does the area between demand and supply through the efficient quantity measure total surplus?
options: Each gap is the market price
The area is seller revenue
Each vertical gap is the gain from one marginal unit
The area is buyer expenditure
hard.feedback: Demand is marginal value and supply is marginal cost.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Demand shifts from D1 to D2. Which statement is correct?
options: Producer surplus falls to zero
Total surplus stays $64
Quantity remains 8
Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all rise; total surplus becomes $100
hard.feedback: The new equilibrium has two $50 surplus triangles.

hard.q: Refer to the graph. Supply shifts from S1 to S2. Which statement is correct?
options: Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and total surplus all fall; total surplus becomes $36
Consumer surplus rises because price rises
Producer surplus rises because price rises
Total surplus stays $64
hard.feedback: Higher marginal cost reduces quantity and both surplus areas.

hard.q: Refer to the step-demand graph. At price $10, how many buyers purchase and what is total consumer surplus?
options: 2 buyers and $13
3 buyers and $15
4 buyers and $20
5 buyers and $10
hard.feedback: The $18, $15, and $12 buyers receive $8, $5, and $2.

hard.q: Refer to the step-supply graph. At price $10, how many sellers participate and what is total producer surplus?
options: 2 sellers and $11
4 sellers and $14
3 sellers and $12
5 sellers and $10
hard.feedback: The $3, $6, and $9 sellers receive $7, $4, and $1.

hard.q: A buyer values a good at $35, pays $20, and seller cost is $11. How is total surplus divided?
options: $20 to the buyer and $4 to the seller
$9 to the buyer and $15 to the seller
$35 to the buyer and $11 to the seller
$15 to the buyer and $9 to the seller
hard.feedback: CS is $15 and PS is $9.

hard.q: A buyer values a good at $35 and the seller's cost is $11. If the market price rises from $20 to $26, what changes?
options: Consumer surplus falls $6, producer surplus rises $6, and total surplus stays $24
Consumer and total surplus both fall $6
Producer and total surplus both rise $6
Both sides gain $6
hard.feedback: Price redistributes the fixed value-cost gain.

hard.q: Which claim is strongest about an efficient market outcome?
options: It guarantees equal surplus
It maximizes measured total surplus under the assumptions but need not be the fairest distribution
It proves willingness to pay measures need perfectly
It eliminates every market failure
hard.feedback: Efficiency is conditional and distribution-neutral.

hard.q: A low-income buyer can pay $12 for a vital item while a wealthy buyer will pay $40 for convenience. What limitation appears?
options: Consumer surplus cannot use dollars
Producer surplus is always negative
Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay, not only need
Demand measures seller cost
hard.feedback: Income can constrain measured willingness to pay.

hard.q: A firm has $100 of producer surplus and a $70 fixed lease cost. Accounting profit is:
hard.feedback: Subtract fixed cost from producer surplus.

hard.q: Before a restriction, consumer surplus is $45 and producer surplus is $35. The restriction prevents exchanges with combined gains of $12 and has no other effects. What is total surplus afterward?
hard.feedback: Initial total surplus is $45 + $35 = $80. The prevented beneficial exchanges remove $12, leaving $68. The question specifies that the reported CS and PS precede the restriction.

hard.q: A price ceiling transfers $18 from producers to consumers and prevents $7 of gains. Total surplus:
options: Rises by $18
Falls by $7
Falls by $25
Is unchanged
hard.feedback: The transfer cancels; the lost gains remain.

hard.q: A tax sends $40 to government revenue and eliminates $9 of gains. Ignoring administration, total surplus:
options: Falls by $49
Rises by $40
Falls by $9
Is unchanged
hard.feedback: Revenue is a transfer; eliminated gains are a loss.

hard.q: A scarce good is allocated to the buyers with the highest willingness to pay. Which limitation of surplus analysis should be kept in mind?
options: Surplus analysis cannot compare alternative allocations.
Market prices eliminate all distributional concerns.
Willingness to pay measures need independently of income.
Willingness to pay can reflect ability to pay as well as preferences, so measured efficiency does not by itself settle fairness.
hard.feedback: Willingness to pay is measured in dollars and can be constrained by purchasing power. A surplus-maximizing allocation can therefore be efficient without resolving questions of need or fairness.

hard.q: Market A has consumer surplus of $80 and producer surplus of $70, but production creates $40 of external damage. Market B has consumer surplus of $75 and producer surplus of $65 with no external damage. Which statement is strongest?
options: B is necessarily unfair because producer surplus is lower
External damage should be ignored because it is outside buyer and seller surplus
Private surplus favors A, but including the stated external damage gives B higher social surplus
A is necessarily socially efficient because its private surplus is larger
hard.feedback: A has $150 private surplus but $110 after the external cost; B has $140 and no stated external cost.

hard.q: Two allocations produce the same total surplus. Allocation X gives almost all gains to one household; Allocation Y distributes gains across many households. Which conclusion is economically defensible from surplus data alone?
options: The allocations cannot have equal total surplus if distributions differ
They are tied on measured efficiency, while choosing between distributions requires an equity judgment
X is more efficient because concentrated gains are larger per person
Y is more efficient because more people receive gains
hard.feedback: Total surplus measures the size of the pie; distribution of the pie is a separate criterion.

elite.q: A price rises by $5. Ten existing buyers continue, and two buyers leave. Why can the consumer-surplus loss exceed $50?
options: Continuing buyers lose $50, and departing buyers lose their former surplus too
Multiply $5 by every potential buyer
Producer surplus is subtracted twice
Total surplus always falls by $5
elite.feedback: The loss includes the rectangle on continuing units plus lost surplus of exiting buyers.

elite.q: A price falls by $4. Eight sellers continue, and two high-cost sellers exit. Why can the producer-surplus loss exceed $32?
options: Multiply $4 by all firms
Continuing sellers lose $32, and exiting sellers lose their former surplus too
Consumer surplus is counted as a seller loss
Total surplus always falls by $4
elite.feedback: The loss includes continuing and exiting sellers.

elite.q: Consumer surplus falls $60, producer surplus rises $44, and revenue rises $10. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $16
Rises by $54
Falls by $6
Falls by $26
elite.feedback: Include government revenue once: −$60 + $44 + $10 = −$6. The $10 received by government is a transfer of surplus, not another loss. Total surplus falls by $6.

elite.q: Consumer surplus rises $35, producer surplus falls $50, and administration uses $4 of resources. Total surplus:
options: Falls by $15
Rises by $31
Falls by $54
Falls by $19
elite.feedback: The consumer and producer changes sum to $35 − $50 = −$15. Administration consumes another $4 of real resources, so the total change is −$19. A resource cost reduces surplus; it is not just a payment transferred to another participant.

elite.q: Why is “a higher price always benefits society” wrong?
options: A higher price can redistribute surplus and alter quantity; total surplus is what matters
Higher prices always reduce producer surplus
Higher prices erase willingness to pay
Society benefits only when consumer surplus is zero
elite.feedback: Price alone does not determine efficiency.

elite.q: Why is “a lower price always benefits society” wrong?
options: Lower prices always raise cost
Consumers may gain while producers lose, and quantity effects can change total gains
Lower prices erase demand
Society benefits only when producer surplus is zero
elite.feedback: Count both sides and quantity effects.

elite.q: Marginal willingness to pay is $18 and marginal cost is $12. Which adjustment raises surplus?
options: Decrease output
Keep output fixed because price is absent
Increase output; the next unit adds $6
Raise price without changing output
elite.feedback: MB exceeds MC by $6.

elite.q: Marginal willingness to pay is $14 and marginal cost is $21. Which adjustment raises surplus?
options: Increase output
Keep output fixed because both are positive
Lower price without changing output
Decrease output; the last unit destroys $7
elite.feedback: MC exceeds MB by $7.

elite.q: Allocation A gives two units to buyers valuing them at $40 and $32; B gives them to buyers valuing them at $35 and $28. Costs are equal. Which is better?
options: Allocation A by $9
Allocation B by $9
Allocation A by $5
They are equal
elite.feedback: A has $72 value versus $63.

elite.q: Plan A uses sellers with costs $9 and $15; Plan B uses costs $12 and $19. Buyers are unchanged. Which is better?
options: Plan B by $7
Plan A by $7
Plan A by $3
They are equal
elite.feedback: A costs $24 versus $31.

elite.q: Buyer value is $50, seller cost is $20, and price is $47. Which statement is correct?
options: Total surplus is $47
Buyer gets $30 and seller gets $20
Total surplus is $30, split $3 to the buyer and $27 to the seller
High price reduces total surplus to $3
elite.feedback: Value minus cost is $30; price divides it.

elite.q: A buyer values a good at $50 and the seller's cost is $20. At a market price of $23, which statement is correct?
options: Total surplus rises to $54
Total surplus falls to $7
Both parties get $30
Total surplus remains $30, split $27 to the buyer and $3 to the seller
elite.feedback: Changing price within the bargaining range redistributes the gain.

elite.q: A seller has marginal cost $12 per unit and a $1,000 fixed license fee. Why can producer surplus be positive while profit is negative?
options: Producer surplus may cover variable costs but not the fixed fee
Producer surplus subtracts the fee twice
Profit ignores fixed costs
Marginal cost includes all fixed costs
elite.feedback: Fixed cost can exceed producer surplus.

elite.q: Why is a triangle formula wrong for a step-shaped demand curve?
options: Step demand has no value information
The surplus region is a sum of rectangles
Consumer surplus cannot be graphed
Price must be zero
elite.feedback: Discrete unit surplus is rectangular.

elite.q: Why can two markets with the same equilibrium price and quantity have different consumer surplus?
options: Consumer surplus depends only on price and quantity
Producer surplus determines it
Demand can have different heights above the common price
Equilibrium equalizes it
elite.feedback: The entire demand region matters.

elite.q: Why can two markets with the same equilibrium price and quantity have different producer surplus?
options: Producer surplus depends only on price and quantity
Consumer surplus determines it
Equilibrium equalizes it
Supply can have different heights below the common price
elite.feedback: The entire supply region matters.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. Why is producer surplus zero even though firms receive revenue?
options: Price equals marginal cost on every traded unit
Demand slopes downward
Quantity is positive
Consumer surplus absorbs revenue
elite.feedback: Every unit has cost equal to price.

elite.q: Refer to the graph. What is total surplus and who receives it?
options: $72, all as producer surplus
$72, all as consumer surplus
$36 split equally
elite.feedback: The consumer-surplus triangle is $72 and producer surplus is zero.

elite.q: A scarce good goes to the highest bidders. What concern can remain despite maximum measured surplus?
options: The allocation cannot be efficient
Producer surplus must be negative
Low-income buyers may have high need but limited dollar willingness to pay
Price cannot be observed
elite.feedback: Measured willingness to pay does not fully resolve need or fairness.

elite.q: Which statement is an efficiency claim?
options: Every buyer should receive the same quantity
Low-income buyers deserve priority
Gains should be split equally
Reassigning production to lower-cost sellers raises total surplus
elite.feedback: Lower cost is an efficiency argument.

elite.q: Which statement is an equity claim?
options: A larger share of gains should go to lower-income households
Highest-value buyers should receive units
Lowest-cost sellers should produce
Exchange continues while value exceeds cost
elite.feedback: Distribution across income groups is equity.

elite.q: A tax leaves $40 consumer surplus, $30 producer surplus, and $20 revenue. Without it, total surplus is $100. Deadweight loss is:
elite.feedback: Post-tax total is $90.

elite.q: A ceiling increases surplus for continuing buyers by $25, but buyers who lose access forfeit $5 of prior surplus. Producer surplus falls by $40. There are no search costs or other effects. What happens to total surplus?
options: It falls by $15
It rises by $20
It falls by $20
It falls by $70
elite.feedback: Count all consumers: their net change is +$25 − $5 = +$20. Adding the $40 producer loss gives a $20 total-surplus loss. Counting only successful buyers understates the loss.

elite.q: Why is the entire producer loss from a price ceiling not necessarily deadweight loss?
options: Producer losses never matter
All consumer gains are deadweight loss
Deadweight loss equals price
Part may be transferred to buyers; only net destroyed gains are deadweight loss
elite.feedback: Separate transfers from destroyed gains.

elite.q: Consumer surplus falls by $70 and producer surplus falls by $50 after a tax, while tax revenue equals $100. What is the reduction in total surplus?
elite.feedback: The $120 decline in private surplus includes $100 transferred as revenue, leaving a $20 reduction in total surplus.

elite.q: A student calls the highest-surplus buyer the marginal buyer. What is wrong?
options: The marginal buyer is a seller
The marginal buyer is at the cutoff and usually has the smallest nonnegative surplus
Consumer surplus cannot be ranked
The highest-value buyer never buys
elite.feedback: The marginal buyer is just willing to purchase.

elite.q: A student calls the lowest-cost seller the marginal seller. What is wrong?
options: The marginal seller is a buyer
Producer surplus cannot be ranked
The marginal seller is the highest-cost seller still trading
The lowest-cost seller never sells
elite.feedback: The marginal seller is at the participation cutoff.

elite.q: A buyer values a unit at $31 and a seller can provide it at a cost of $18. What total gain from exchange is available?
options: The buyer must receive all $13
The seller must receive all $13
The market price must equal $13
The trade can create $13 in total gains
elite.feedback: Buyer value minus seller cost gives the total gain from the exchange: $31 − $18 = $13.

elite.q: A buyer values a unit at $42, the seller’s cost is $26, and the price is $34. Which complete statement is correct?
options: Consumer surplus is $8, producer surplus is $8, and total surplus is $16
Consumer surplus is $16 and producer surplus is $8
Consumer surplus is $8 and total surplus is $34
Producer surplus is $16 and total surplus is $42
elite.feedback: The price divides the $16 gain: $42 − $34 = $8 for the buyer and $34 − $26 = $8 for the seller.

elite.q: A $3 per-unit tax lowers private surplus by $45 and creates $36 in tax revenue. What happened to total surplus?
options: It fell by $45
It fell by $9
It rose by $36
It was unchanged
elite.feedback: The $45 private-surplus reduction includes a $36 transfer to tax revenue, leaving a $9 reduction in total surplus.

4 units and $39

3 trades; the last accepted buyer values the unit at $19 and the last accepted seller costs $16
2 trades because only trades with gains above $10 count
3 trades; the lowest-value buyer and highest-cost seller define the cutoff

legendary.q: A linear market has demand P = 28 − Q and supply P = 4 + Q. Demand then becomes P = 32 − Q. With supply unchanged, which statement correctly compares the two equilibria?

Price rises by $4, while CS rises by $26 and TS rises by $26
Price rises by $2, while CS rises by $2 and TS rises by $4
legendary.feedback: Initially Q = 12 and P = $16, giving CS = PS = $72. After the demand change, Q = 14 and P = $18, giving CS = PS = $98. CS rises by $26 and TS by $52. Higher willingness to pay changes the surplus comparison even though the price rises.

legendary.q: Demand is P = 27 − Q. Supply changes from P = 3 + Q to P = 7 + Q because production costs rise. Which comparison correctly separates producer surplus from price changes?

Price rises by $4, while PS falls by $22 and TS falls by $22
Price rises by $2, but PS falls by $22 and TS falls by $44
Price rises by $2, so PS rises by $24 and TS rises by $48
legendary.feedback: The original equilibrium is Q = 12, P = $15, with CS = PS = $72. After the cost increase, Q = 10 and P = $17, with CS = PS = $50. Thus PS falls $22 and TS falls $44. The higher selling price does not offset higher costs and fewer trades.

legendary.q: Demand rises from P = 24 − Q to P = 28 − Q while supply remains P = 4 + Q. At the new efficient equilibrium, total surplus is $44 higher. How is this increase explained?

$20 transferred from sellers and $24 from additional trades
$40 of additional spending and $4 of tax revenue
$40 of higher value on the original ten units and $4 from additional trades
legendary.feedback: The original efficient quantity is 10 and the new quantity is 12. Willingness to pay rises $4 on each of the original ten units, adding $40. The two new units add a triangle of 0.5 × 2 × $4 = $4. A demand increase can raise gains on existing units as well as create new beneficial trades.

legendary.q: A supply decrease reduces the efficient quantity. Why?
options: Marginal costs are higher, so fewer units have value at least as large as cost
Buyers’ willingness to pay becomes zero
The demand curve stops measuring value
Every remaining seller earns zero surplus
legendary.feedback: When marginal cost rises, the positive-gain range of output shrinks.

legendary.q: A rule changes the market price but not the set of completed trades. Which test prevents confusing redistribution with an efficiency change?
options: Check whether consumers paid a lower price
Check whether any units with positive value-minus-cost gains were added or lost
Check whether producers received a higher price
Check whether consumer and producer surplus are equal
legendary.feedback: Efficiency changes when the set of beneficial trades changes; price alone can merely redistribute surplus.

boss.q: Which statement best defends competitive efficiency?
options: Everyone receives equal surplus
Price is always fair
All value-above-cost units trade and value-below-cost units do not
No policy can ever help
boss.feedback: Competitive efficiency requires every unit with buyer value above seller cost to trade, while units with value below cost should not be produced.

boss.q: Which statement best limits competitive efficiency?
options: It requires equal CS and PS
It applies only at zero price
It proves WTP equals need
It depends on assumptions and does not settle distributional fairness
boss.feedback: Competitive surplus maximization depends on the model’s assumptions and addresses efficiency; it does not by itself determine whether the distribution of gains is fair.

boss.q: Buyer value is $52, seller cost $18, and price $45. How is surplus divided?

boss.q: Why is a producer-surplus loss not necessarily a social loss of equal size?
options: Producer surplus never matters
Consumer surplus always falls more
Some may be transferred to consumers or government
Social loss equals revenue
boss.feedback: A loss of producer surplus can be partly or fully transferred to consumers or the government. Only surplus that disappears is a social loss.

boss.q: Why is a consumer-surplus gain not necessarily a social gain of equal size?
options: Consumer surplus never matters
Producer surplus always rises too
Social gain equals price
It may come from a transfer out of producer surplus
boss.feedback: A gain in consumer surplus can come from a transfer out of producer surplus. Social gain depends on the net change in total surplus.

Becomes equal to revenue
