boss.feedback: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 100 thousand imports.

boss.q: A $10 tariff applies to 20 imports. Revenue equals:
boss.feedback: Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by post-tariff imports: $10 × 20 = $200.

boss.q: A tariff raises Qs from 10 to 20 and lowers Qd from 50 to 40. Imports fall from:
boss.feedback: Before the tariff, imports are 50 − 10 = 40. After the tariff, imports are 40 − 20 = 20, so imports fall from 40 to 20.

boss.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the production-distortion loss?
boss.feedback: The production-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

boss.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the consumption-distortion loss?
boss.feedback: The consumption-distortion triangle has area ½ × $10 × 10 = $50.

boss.q: Refer to the tariff graph. What is the total deadweight loss?
boss.feedback: The $50 production-distortion loss and $50 consumption-distortion loss sum to $100 of deadweight loss.

boss.q: A quota of 20 creates a $10 price gap. Quota rent equals:
boss.feedback: Quota rent equals the price gap per imported unit multiplied by the permitted imports: $10 × 20 = $200.

boss.q: Who receives quota rent when licenses are auctioned?
options: The government
Foreign exporters automatically
Consumers automatically
No one
boss.feedback: When the government auctions the import licenses, the auction proceeds capture the quota rents for the government.

boss.q: Who receives quota rent when free licenses go to foreign exporters?
options: The domestic government
The foreign license holders
Domestic consumers
All domestic firms
boss.feedback: When foreign exporters receive the import licenses for free, those foreign license holders capture the quota rents.

boss.q: What is fixed by a tariff?
options: The exact import quantity
Domestic demand
The price wedge per imported unit
The world supply curve
boss.feedback: A per-unit tariff fixes the price wedge between the world price and the tariff-inclusive domestic price; the quantity of imports can adjust.

boss.q: What is fixed by an import quota?
options: The exact domestic price under all shocks
The tariff rate
Domestic producer surplus
The maximum import quantity
boss.feedback: A binding import quota fixes the maximum quantity that may be imported; the domestic price can adjust to make the import gap equal that cap.

boss.q: Why can demand growth raise price more under a quota?
options: Imports cannot expand beyond the cap
The world price disappears
Domestic supply becomes vertical
Quota rents must become zero
boss.feedback: Because imports cannot expand beyond the quota, stronger demand must be absorbed through a higher domestic price rather than additional imports.

boss.q: Which tariff component is a transfer?
options: Production distortion
Government revenue
Consumption distortion
Both distortion triangles
boss.feedback: Government tariff revenue is a transfer within national welfare accounting. The production and consumption distortion triangles are deadweight losses.

boss.q: Which statement best evaluates a jobs argument?
options: Count only protected jobs
Ignore prices

Assume retaliation cannot occur
boss.feedback: A complete jobs argument must consider the protected jobs along with higher consumer costs, effects on downstream industries, resource reallocation, and possible retaliation.

boss.q: Which statement best evaluates national security?
options: Protect every industry
Ignore the risk entirely
Count only imports
Compare the specific risk with targeted alternatives and costs
boss.feedback: A national-security argument is strongest when it identifies a specific strategic vulnerability and compares protection with narrower, less costly ways to address that risk.

boss.q: Which fact weakens infant-industry protection?
options: Costs do not fall after prolonged protection
The industry is young
Imports exist
Consumers like low prices
boss.feedback: The infant-industry argument depends on temporary protection producing learning and lower future costs. If costs do not fall after prolonged protection, that rationale is weakened.

boss.q: What can retaliation do?
options: Guarantee lower tariffs
Reduce the country’s exports
Eliminate consumer losses
Increase every domestic wage
boss.feedback: Trading partners may respond with restrictions of their own, reducing the protected country’s exports and spreading losses to additional industries and workers.

Exports in another market
repairQuestions.feedback: Importer status follows the price comparison, not demand size alone.

repairQuestions.q: A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?
options: Domestic demand must be zero
A tariff must be imposed
The country must ban imports
The world price must be above the domestic no-trade equilibrium price
repairQuestions.feedback: Export status depends on the world-price comparison.

repairQuestions.q: Domestic consumers demand 70 units and firms supply 25 at the world price. A student reports 70 imports. Correct the calculation.
options: 45 imports
25 imports
70 imports
95 imports
repairQuestions.feedback: Imports are 70−25=45.

repairQuestions.q: Domestic firms supply 64 units and consumers demand 22 at the world price. A student reports 64 exports. Correct the calculation.
options: 22 exports
42 exports
64 exports
86 exports
repairQuestions.feedback: Exports are 64−22=42.

repairQuestions.q: A student sees producer losses from imports and concludes total surplus must fall. What corrects the error?
options: Producer losses are not real
Imports never lower producer surplus
Consumer gains can exceed producer losses
Government revenue always offsets the loss
repairQuestions.feedback: Net welfare depends on both sides of the market.

repairQuestions.q: Why do consumers gain when a lower world price opens an import market?
options: They pay more and purchase less
Domestic supply shifts right automatically
Tariff revenue rises
They pay less and purchase more
repairQuestions.feedback: Both the price and quantity effects raise consumer surplus.

repairQuestions.q: A student says exports benefit everyone because producers gain. What is the correction?
options: Domestic consumers may lose from the higher price
Producers never gain from exports
The domestic price falls
Exports eliminate domestic consumption
repairQuestions.feedback: Export gains are unevenly distributed.

repairQuestions.q: Why can total surplus rise even when domestic consumers lose from exports?
options: Consumer losses are ignored
Producer gains can exceed consumer losses
Foreign surplus is counted as domestic government revenue
Domestic demand becomes vertical
repairQuestions.feedback: The net change is what matters for total surplus.

repairQuestions.q: A student says “gains from trade” means every person gains. What does the term actually mean?
options: Every wage rises
Every producer expands
Total surplus rises
Imports and exports are equal
repairQuestions.feedback: Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.

repairQuestions.q: Why does possible compensation not prove losers are compensated?
options: Compensation occurs automatically through the world price
Losers have no measurable loss
Total surplus cannot fund transfers
A transfer requires an actual policy or agreement
repairQuestions.feedback: Feasibility and implementation are different.

repairQuestions.q: A student predicts a tariff will lower the domestic price. What is the correct basic-model prediction?
options: The price rises by the tariff above the world price
The price falls by the tariff
The price stays at the world price
The price becomes zero
repairQuestions.feedback: The tariff creates an upward price wedge.

repairQuestions.q: A tariff raises domestic production and lowers domestic consumption. What happens to imports?
options: They rise
They fall
They are unchanged
They equal domestic production
repairQuestions.feedback: The gap between demand and supply shrinks.

repairQuestions.q: A student labels tariff revenue as deadweight loss. What is wrong?
options: Revenue belongs to consumers
Deadweight loss equals producer gain
Revenue is a transfer; deadweight loss is lost surplus
Tariffs never collect revenue
repairQuestions.feedback: Separate transfers from net losses.

repairQuestions.q: Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
options: Producer surplus and tariff revenue
Imports and exports
Consumer surplus and quota rent
Production distortion and consumption distortion
repairQuestions.feedback: The tariff causes too much high-cost domestic production and too little consumption.

repairQuestions.q: A student says a binding quota leaves price at the world price. What is the correction?
options: The domestic price rises until the import gap equals the quota
The world price rises by law
Domestic supply becomes zero
Demand becomes perfectly elastic
repairQuestions.feedback: The price adjusts to ration the limited imports.

repairQuestions.q: A student assumes the government always receives quota rents. What determines the recipient?
options: The demand-curve intercept only
Ownership or auction of the import licenses
The no-trade quantity only
The tariff rate
repairQuestions.feedback: Quota rents follow the license rights.

repairQuestions.q: A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?
options: A tariff fixes domestic demand
A quota fixes the world price
A tariff fixes the wedge while a quota fixes import quantity
Both fix producer surplus
repairQuestions.feedback: Different policy instruments adjust differently to shocks.

repairQuestions.q: If foreign exporters receive quota rents, why can a quota be worse for national welfare than an equivalent tariff?
options: The quota lowers the domestic price
The tariff creates no consumer loss
The quota increases free-trade imports
The rent transfer leaves the importing country
repairQuestions.feedback: Rent allocation changes national welfare.

repairQuestions.q: What is missing from the claim “protection saves jobs”?
options: Effects on consumers, downstream industries, exports, and alternative uses of resources
The protected industry’s name
The number of foreign countries only
A promise that prices never change
repairQuestions.feedback: A complete analysis includes opportunity costs and spillovers.

repairQuestions.q: What is the proper response to a national-security claim?
options: Accept every claim automatically
Evaluate the specific risk, policy cost, and narrower alternatives
Reject every claim automatically
Count only tariff revenue
repairQuestions.feedback: Security arguments require evidence and proportionality.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says the world price is the same thing as the country’s no-trade equilibrium price. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The world price is the external trading price; comparing it with the no-trade price reveals importer or exporter status
The world price should be treated as the domestic equilibrium price after trade, so the two prices coincide by definition
The world price measures domestic producer surplus, while the no-trade price measures domestic consumer surplus
The no-trade price is determined by foreign supply conditions, while the world price comes from domestic supply and demand
repairQuestions.feedback: Trade status comes from comparing the world price with the domestic autarky equilibrium price.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calculates imports as domestic supply minus domestic demand. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Imports equal supply plus demand
Imports equal world price minus domestic price
Imports equal domestic production only
Imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied
repairQuestions.feedback: In an importing market, excess domestic demand is filled by imports.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calculates exports as domestic demand minus domestic supply. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Exports equal world price times domestic demand
Exports equal domestic consumption only
Exports equal domestic quantity supplied minus domestic quantity demanded
Exports equal demand plus supply
repairQuestions.feedback: In an exporting market, excess domestic supply is sold abroad.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says opening an importing market to a lower world price reduces domestic consumption. What is the correction?
options: Only production can change with trade
The lower domestic price generally increases quantity demanded
The lower price decreases quantity demanded
Consumption is fixed after trade opens
repairQuestions.feedback: Consumers respond to the lower price by demanding more.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says a lower world price in an importing market increases domestic production. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: The lower domestic price generally reduces quantity supplied by domestic firms
A lower price always raises domestic production
Domestic output is fixed by the world price
Imports cannot affect domestic producers
repairQuestions.feedback: Domestic producers move along supply to a lower quantity at the lower price.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says free trade cannot create net gains if one domestic group loses. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Distributional losses are never counted
Net gains can be positive when winners gain more than losers lose
Any losing group makes total surplus negative
Trade gains require every person to gain
repairQuestions.feedback: Aggregate gains and distribution are separate: a market can have positive net gains and identifiable losers.

repairQuestions.q: A learner calculates tariff revenue using all domestic consumption rather than imported units. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Multiply the tariff by domestic production plus imports
Use the world price times all consumption
Tariff revenue equals consumer surplus lost
Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported
repairQuestions.feedback: The tariff is collected on imported units, not on every unit consumed.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says all consumer surplus lost under a tariff is deadweight loss. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Producer gains are not part of total surplus
Government revenue is always deadweight loss
Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
All consumer loss disappears from national welfare
repairQuestions.feedback: Tariff welfare analysis separates transfers from production and consumption distortions.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says quota rent is automatically government revenue. Which statement best corrects this mistake?
options: Quota rent is always collected as a tariff
Quota rent equals domestic producer surplus
Quota rent exists only when the quota is nonbinding
Quota rent goes to whoever holds the valuable import rights unless the government auctions them
repairQuestions.feedback: Unlike tariff revenue, quota rent depends on who receives or buys the import licenses.

repairQuestions.q: A learner says equal-price tariffs and quotas must have identical national effects. What key issue is missing?
options: Whether imports exist
Whether domestic firms produce anything
Who receives the quota rents
Whether consumers face a price
repairQuestions.feedback: If foreign license holders capture quota rents, national surplus differs from an equivalent tariff with domestic government revenue.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does consumer surplus connect to an import market?
options: It becomes tariff revenue
It equals domestic production
A lower world price expands the area below demand and above price
It disappears whenever imports occur
bridgeQuestions.feedback: In an importing market, the lower world price increases consumer surplus by lowering the price buyers pay and increasing the quantity they purchase.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does producer surplus connect to an import market?
options: It always becomes zero
It equals imports
It becomes consumer expenditure
A lower domestic price shrinks the area above supply and below price
bridgeQuestions.feedback: In an importing market, the lower world price reduces producer surplus because domestic sellers receive a lower price and sell a smaller quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does total surplus identify gains from trade?
options: Compare consumer plus producer surplus before and after trade
Compare imports with exports only
Count producer revenue only
Count the physical number of goods leaving
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Gains from trade equal the increase in total domestic surplus, found by comparing consumer plus producer surplus before and after trade.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can trade raise total surplus while hurting one group?
options: Group losses are not counted
A larger gain to one side can exceed the other side’s loss
Prices do not affect surplus
Total surplus measures equality
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Trade can raise total surplus when the gains to the winning side exceed the losses borne by the losing side.

bridgeQuestions.q: What surplus concept separates tariff revenue from deadweight loss?
options: All consumer losses are deadweight loss
All producer gains are deadweight loss
Transfers change recipients; deadweight loss removes mutually beneficial trades
Revenue is never part of welfare
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Tariff revenue is a transfer to the government, while deadweight loss represents gains from trade that disappear because the tariff distorts production and consumption.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the demand curve determine imports at the world price?
options: It gives foreign supply
It fixes tariff revenue
It gives quota ownership
It gives domestic quantity demanded
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At the world price, the demand curve gives domestic quantity demanded. Imports are the amount by which quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the supply curve determine imports at the world price?
options: It gives domestic quantity supplied
It gives world quantity demanded
It fixes consumer surplus
It gives foreign income
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At the world price, the supply curve gives domestic quantity supplied. Imports are the amount by which domestic quantity demanded exceeds that quantity.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does Pw below equilibrium create imports?
options: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Both quantities become zero
Demand shifts left by definition
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When the world price is below the no-trade equilibrium price, domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied. Imports fill that excess demand.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why does Pw above equilibrium create exports?
options: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Supply shifts left by definition
Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
The market has a shortage
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When the world price is above the no-trade equilibrium price, domestic quantity supplied exceeds domestic quantity demanded. The excess supply is exported.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does comparative advantage support gains from international trade?
options: It requires absolute advantage in every good
It eliminates scarcity
It guarantees equal gains
Specialization follows lower opportunity cost and exchange expands consumption possibilities
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Comparative advantage identifies the goods each side can produce at lower opportunity cost. Specialization on that basis can create gains that exchange allows both sides to share.

bridgeQuestions.q: Can a country gain from trade if it is less productive in every good?
options: Yes, if opportunity costs differ and it specializes by comparative advantage
No, absolute disadvantage prevents all gains
Only if it bans imports
Only if wages are identical
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Yes. Even a country with an absolute disadvantage in every good can gain from trade when opportunity costs differ and it specializes according to comparative advantage.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why is opportunity cost central to specialization?
options: It measures tariff revenue
It identifies which production sacrifice is smaller
It determines quota ownership
It equals the world price in every market
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Opportunity cost measures what must be given up to produce a good. Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can demand elasticity affect consumer losses from an export-driven price increase?
options: Elasticity fixes the world price
Elasticity determines license ownership
More responsive quantity demanded changes the lost-consumption area and surplus reduction
Elasticity makes consumer surplus constant
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When demand is more elastic, domestic quantity demanded responds more to an export-driven price increase, changing the size of the consumer-surplus loss.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can supply elasticity affect domestic production response to a tariff?
options: Elasticity eliminates tariff revenue
Elasticity fixes import quantity under every policy
Elasticity makes marginal cost irrelevant
More responsive supply creates a larger production increase and distortion
bridgeQuestions.feedback: When domestic supply is more responsive to price, the tariff-induced price increase produces a larger increase in domestic output and therefore a larger production distortion, other things equal.

bridgeQuestions.q: How is a tariff connected to a tax wedge?
options: It creates a gap between the domestic buyer price and the world resource price
It creates a gap between two domestic currencies
It makes imports free
It sets producer surplus to zero
bridgeQuestions.feedback: In the small-country model, the tariff creates a wedge between the world price and the higher domestic price paid and received in the protected market.

bridgeQuestions.q: How is tariff deadweight loss connected to lost gains from exchange?
options: It equals tariff revenue
The tariff prevents beneficial imports and induces higher-cost production
It equals all consumer expenditure
It is a payment to foreign firms
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The tariff prevents some imports whose value to domestic buyers exceeds their world resource cost and also induces higher-cost domestic production. Those foregone gains create deadweight loss.

bridgeQuestions.q: How can trade move consumption beyond a country’s production possibilities frontier?
options: Trade moves domestic production outside physical constraints
A tariff expands resources automatically
Specialization and exchange separate what is consumed from what is domestically produced
Imports eliminate opportunity cost
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Trade does not move domestic production beyond the PPF. Specialization and exchange can instead allow the country to consume a combination of goods that it could not produce by itself.

bridgeQuestions.q: What does the PPF contribute to trade analysis?
options: It directly calculates tariff revenue
It fixes the world price
It identifies quota rents
It shows opportunity costs and the production tradeoffs behind comparative advantage
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The PPF shows the production tradeoffs that determine opportunity costs. Those opportunity costs help identify comparative advantage and the basis for specialization.

bridgeQuestions.q: What efficiency question should be separated from the equity question in trade?
options: Whether total surplus rises versus how gains and losses are distributed
Whether imports equal exports versus whether prices exist
Whether firms earn revenue versus whether consumers buy
Whether quotas are legal versus whether supply slopes upward
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Efficiency asks whether trade raises total surplus. Equity asks how the resulting gains and losses are distributed across people, firms, industries, or regions.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why might adjustment assistance be discussed even when trade raises total surplus?
options: Trade eliminates all consumer gains
Some workers and communities can bear concentrated transition costs
Efficiency requires equal outcomes
Imports always reduce total employment
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Trade can raise total surplus while imposing concentrated transition costs on particular workers and communities. Adjustment assistance addresses those distributional costs without denying the aggregate gains.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the import quantity connect to ordinary market disequilibrium at the world price?
options: Imports are the same as a domestic shortage under a binding ceiling
Imports equal total domestic production
Imports are unrelated to supply and demand
Imports fill the gap between domestic quantity demanded and domestic quantity supplied
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At the world price, excess domestic demand is met through imports.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does export quantity connect to ordinary supply-and-demand analysis at the world price?
options: Exports occur only when domestic supply shifts left
Exports are determined without reference to price
Exports are the excess of domestic quantity supplied over domestic quantity demanded
Exports equal domestic quantity demanded
bridgeQuestions.feedback: At the world price, excess domestic supply is sold to foreign buyers.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does the surplus framework connect free-trade winners and losers to the efficiency conclusion?
options: Add consumer and producer surplus changes to determine the net gain
Count only the group that gains
Ignore producer surplus in importing markets
Treat every redistribution as deadweight loss
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a tariff connect to the tax-wedge idea from domestic markets?
options: It guarantees the legal and economic burden are identical
It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
It eliminates the role of price
It shifts world demand only
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A tariff acts like a tax on imports and raises the domestic price above the world price in the small-country model.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does tariff deadweight loss connect to surplus analysis?
options: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
It is the full transfer from consumers to producers
It equals tariff revenue
It is producer surplus after the tariff
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The surplus framework identifies the trades and resource uses that no longer maximize gains.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a binding quota connect to ordinary supply-and-demand pressure?
options: Import restrictions make domestic supply irrelevant
Restricting imports reduces available supply to the domestic market and raises the domestic price
A quota shifts domestic demand left automatically
A quota fixes the world price and domestic price at zero
bridgeQuestions.feedback: The quantity restriction tightens the domestic market and raises price until the permitted import gap is satisfied.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does quota rent connect to economic rent more generally?
options: A scarce legal right can acquire value because it permits profitable access
Quota rent is a payment for labor only
Economic rent requires a perfectly competitive labor market
Quota rent equals consumer surplus by definition
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Import licenses become valuable because the restriction creates a price gap.

bridgeQuestions.q: Why can auctioning quota licenses make a quota look more like a tariff in national-welfare accounting?
options: Auctioning eliminates the domestic price increase
Auctioning makes imports unlimited
Auctioning turns the quota into an export subsidy
The government captures the quota rent much like tariff revenue
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Who receives the rent is a major difference between quotas and tariffs.

bridgeQuestions.q: A demand increase occurs under a fixed quota. What does the quota teach about quantity controls versus price-based barriers?
options: Both price and imports must stay unchanged
The quota automatically becomes a tariff
The import quantity stays capped while domestic price can rise further
Domestic price stays fixed while imports expand freely
bridgeQuestions.feedback: A hard quantity limit adjusts differently from a fixed per-unit tariff when market conditions change.

bridgeQuestions.q: If foreign exporters capture the quota rents, what distributional issue should policy analysis consider?
options: Whether the world price becomes the autarky price
Whether part of the domestic consumer loss becomes income to foreigners rather than domestic revenue
Whether domestic demand becomes perfectly elastic
Whether producer surplus is always zero
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Rent ownership affects the national distribution and welfare consequences of a quota.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does a quota-versus-tariff comparison connect to policy design?
options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
All trade restrictions have identical distributional effects
Only quotas create deadweight loss
Tariffs never affect domestic producers
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Policy evaluation must track both efficiency distortions and the destination of rents or revenue.

bridgeQuestions.q: How does evaluating protection connect positive and normative economics?
options: Positive economics decides which distribution is fair
Normative economics calculates tariff revenue mechanically
The two approaches are identical in trade policy
Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
bridgeQuestions.feedback: Trade-policy evaluation separates what a policy does from judgments about whether its goals justify those effects.
